facets.text: A post town on the frontier of Transylvania, named by Count Dracula, where Harker stops.

Bistritz is a town in Transylvania, near the frontier, in the Carpathian mountains. It is an old place with a stormy past, marked by fires and a long siege, and it is where the narrator stops on the way to Count Dracula's domain. Its inn, the Golden Krone Hotel, is run by a cheery elderly woman who expects the traveller.

Bistritz is a frontier town in Transylvania, set in the Carpathian mountains near the Borgo Pass, and an old place marked by great fires and a long siege. It is where the narrator stops on the way to Count Dracula's domain, and its Golden Krone Hotel, run by a cheery elderly woman, expects him. The town's people seem to regard the journey with fear, and it is named as the post town Count Dracula gave.

The Danube is a broad, deep river in eastern Europe, crossed by a bridge the narrator passes on his journey through Buda-Pesth. In the Count's account it is the frontier that Dracula-family leaders crossed to fight the Turks on their own ground, so it marks a long history of warfare.

The Danube is a broad, deep river in eastern Europe, crossed by a bridge near Buda-Pesth. In the Count's telling it is the frontier his Dracula forebears crossed to beat the Turks on their own ground. Ships that sail the Black Sea reach it at its mouth, which the company expects the Count to make for.

The Danube is a broad, deep river in eastern Europe, crossed by a fine bridge at Buda-Pesth. In the Count's telling it is the frontier his Dracula forebears crossed to beat the Turks on their own ground. Ships from the Black Sea reach it at its mouth, and the crew of the Czarina Catherine said that they feared the river itself.
The mountain range through which Harker travels, said to gather many superstitions.

Carpathians is a mountain range in Transylvania, seen by Jonathan Harker as a wild, forested chain of steep peaks, snow-capped summits and dark passes. Its horseshoe shape is said by a reader's source to gather many superstitions, and local people cross themselves and make warding gestures near it.
Someone Harker keeps notes for, planning to share his travels with her.
Is visiting Whitby, where she meets Lucy at the station and keeps a journal.
Now married to Jonathan Harker and living at Exeter, writing to Lucy about their new life.
Now married to Jonathan Harker, Mina keeps her shorthand practice and a journal, and grieves for Lucy and Mrs. Westenra.
Keeps a typed copy of her journal and has typed Jonathan's journal for Van Helsing to read.
Mina Harker is a pearl among women, as Van Helsing describes her, and is sent to Seward's house after arriving.
Kept out of the vampire-hunting work by her husband and the men, and is now troubled by this exclusion and her weakness.
Bears a burning mark on her forehead from the Sacred Wafer, which she believes marks her as unclean.
Shows a red scar on her forehead, and in the mountains she is drawn toward the three women and is unable to leave the holy circle.

Mina is a young woman whose journal appears in the record, and Jonathan Harker plans to talk over his travels with her. Her own writing is not yet shown in these early passages, so her look and manner are not described here.

Mina is a young woman whom Jonathan Harker writes to and plans to talk over his travels with; she is shown as a writer of journals and shorthand letters. Harker wants to shield her from the horrors he has met, and he counts her as a faithful friend and beloved. Her own speech and look are not yet shown in these passages.

Mina Murray is a young woman, a schoolmistress and Jonathan Harker's sweetheart, whom he writes to in shorthand and plans to share his travels with. She is a diligent writer who practises shorthand and the typewriter, keeps a private journal, and is a close, confiding friend of Lucy Westenra, to whom she writes warmly and at length.

Mina Murray is a young schoolmistress and Jonathan Harker's sweetheart, to whom he writes in shorthand and plans to share his travels. She is a diligent, practical woman who practises shorthand and the typewriter, keeps a private journal, and is a close, confiding friend of Lucy Westenra. She is staying in Whitby, where she meets Lucy and keeps her journal.

Mina is a diligent, practical young woman and close friend of Lucy Westenra, to whom she writes letters and confides. She keeps a private journal and practises shorthand and typing, and she is married to Jonathan Harker, whose journal she has typed. She is careful and observant, and is often anxious about Lucy and Jonathan.

Mina Murray, a diligent and observant young woman and close friend of Lucy Westenra, who confides in her by letter. She keeps a private journal in shorthand, types it, and is engaged to, and later married to, Jonathan Harker. She is described as a pearl among women and is anxious for Lucy and for her husband, while Van Helsing writes to her with urgent requests for help.

A perceptive, diligent young woman who keeps a shorthand journal and types it for the group. Married to Jonathan Harker, she is called a pearl among women by Van Helsing and is kept out of the hunting work by the men, which troubles her. She is close to Lucy Westenra and writes to her in confidence.
The castle of Count Dracula in the Carpathians, whose exact location Harker cannot find on any map.

The castle of Count Dracula in the Carpathians. Its rooms are dusty and disused, its outer door is locked, and its walls are sheer enough that the Count can climb them. A ruined chapel and vaults lie beneath it.

Castle Dracula is a castle in the far east of Transylvania, among the Carpathian mountains near the borders of Moldavia and Bukovina. The passages give no exact location, and no map the narrator found shows it. It is the home of the Count, a nobleman who speaks of it as his own and invites the narrator to visit there.

Castle Dracula is a castle in the wild Carpathian mountains of far eastern Transylvania, near the borders of Moldavia and Bukovina, on no map the narrator has found. It is the home of the Count, who speaks of it as his own and invites the narrator to visit. Its exact location is not given, and it is said to be a place where Mina's husband Jonathan Harker has stayed.
Signs his letter as a friend and calls Harker 'my friend', while arranging his travel to Bukovina and the Borgo Pass.
A nobleman of Transylvania who has summoned Harker to his castle. He writes courteously and his servants and passengers treat his name with dread.
Gives his name as Dracula, has an unnaturally strong and cold grip, and avoids being seen in mirrors.
Has a pale, aquiline face with sharp white teeth, coarse broad hands with hair in the palms, and long pointed nails.
Is a boyar who has long been master in Transylvania and wants to learn English to pass unnoticed in London.
Can climb down the sheer castle wall headfirst like a lizard, with cloak spread like wings.
Has the power to command the vampiric women and holds claim over Harker, showing a terrible fury when crossed.
Lies in a box of earth in the chapel, where he appears dead but for warm cheeks and red lips.
Plans to send Harker home and says he may never meet him again, though he suspects Harker of intentions to leave.
Is the man behind the scattered boxes, moving them to many parts of London and apparently able to handle the earth-boxes himself.
An old man of great physical strength, white moustache and thin frame, who helped carry the boxes.
Appears with a scar on his forehead, waxen face and red eyes, and can flee into mist and turn into a black-clad figure.
Says Mina is now bound to him in blood and will come to his call, and that he can command her across land or sea.
Has escaped from the Piccadilly house by the stable and now flees by sea, carrying his last earth-box aboard a ship.
Described by Mina as a criminal of imperfectly formed mind who flees when his existence is in danger.

A nobleman of Transylvania who writes to Harker as 'my friend' and arranges his travel toward Bukovina and the Borgo Pass. He is anticipated and expected by innkeepers in Bistritz, who are frightened by his name and decline to speak of him. He is said to have a castle in the Carpathians, and his manner in correspondence is courteous and welcoming.

Count Dracula is a Transylvanian nobleman and boyar who writes to Harker as a friend and arranges his journey toward Bukovina and the Borgo Pass. He receives Harker in person at a castle in the Carpathians, where he is a courtly, attentive host who keeps Harker up through the night. Innkeepers in Bistritz fear his name and refuse to speak of him, and he has a strong, cold handshake.

Count Dracula is a Transylvanian boyar and nobleman who lives alone in a remote Carpathian castle, where he keeps Harker as a prisoner, though he has no visible servants. He is courteous and formal in manner, with a pale aquiline face, sharp canine teeth and a powerful, cold grip. He boasts of his ancient, warlike Szekely lineage, and he claims the right to command the wolves and to control the women who attend him. He seems to be planning Harker's departure, and he has taken interest in England, where he has a new estate.

Count Dracula is a Transylvanian boyar and nobleman who lives in a remote Carpathian castle, where he holds Harker prisoner while posing as a courteous host. He has a pale, aquiline face, long white moustache, sharp canine teeth, great physical strength and a cold grip, and has no visible servants, appearing to do the menial work himself. He is said to command wolves and women, and to shape-shift into mist or a black-clad figure. He holds a claim over Mina, who he says is bound to him in blood, and he has an estate in England near London. Lately he is said to have fled England by sea, carrying an earth-box aboard a ship.

Count Dracula is a Transylvanian nobleman and boyar of the Szekely line, a pale, white-moustached old man of great physical strength and cold grip, with sharp canine teeth. He keeps a remote Carpathian castle with no visible servants, is said to command wolves and to turn into mist or a black-clad figure, and claims Mina is bound to him in blood. He sleeps in earth-boxes and is said to have fled England by sea carrying his last earth-box aboard a ship.
A people of eastern and northern Transylvania who claim descent from Attila and the Huns.

The Szekelys are one of the four nationalities of Transylvania, living in the east and north of the country. They claim descent from Attila and the Huns, and the Count speaks of them with pride as a warlike race that guarded frontiers and fought for lordship.
Peasants of the region seen along the road, in picturesque dress, considered harmless by reputation.

Slovaks are a people of the region around Bistritz and the Borgo Pass, seen by the narrator from a moving coach. They are described as wild-looking, with black hair, heavy moustaches, sheepskin coats and staves tipped with axes, yet said to be harmless and rather lacking in self-assertion.

Slovaks are a wild-looking people of the Bistritz and Borgo Pass region, with black hair, heavy moustaches, sheepskin coats, nail-studded belts and staves tipped with axes. They are described as harmless and rather lacking in self-assertion, yet they serve as hired carters who handle the heavy boxes of earth at the castle.

Slovaks are a wild-looking people of the Bistritz and Borgo Pass region, with black hair, heavy moustaches, baggy trousers, studded leather belts and long staves tipped with axes. They are described as harmless and lacking in self-assertion, yet they serve as carters who haul the heavy boxes of earth to the castle and ship them onward. Skinsky, a trader on the Danube, deals with Slovak river traders who carry cargo down to the port.
A mountain pass leading from Bistritz toward Bukovina, through which the coach travels.

Borgo Pass is a mountain pass in the Carpathians, leading from the frontier town of Bistritz into Bukovina. Its narrow, dark gorge is approached at night by the travelling coach, where passengers grow excited and offer the traveller gifts and blessings against evil. It is where a carriage was supposed to meet the traveller, though none arrives there at first.

Borgo Pass is a mountain pass in the Carpathians, leading from the frontier town of Bistritz into Bukovina. Its dark, narrow gorge is entered at night by the travelling coach, whose passengers grow agitated and press protective gifts and blessings on the traveller. It is where a carriage was meant to meet the traveller, though none is there when the coach arrives, and a calèche with black horses later appears beside the coach. The driver says the traveller is not expected after all.

Borgo Pass is a mountain gorge in the Carpathians, leading from the frontier town of Bistritz toward Bukovina. It is entered at night by the travelling coach, whose passengers grow agitated and press gifts and blessings on the traveller. It is where a carriage was meant to meet the traveller, though none is there on arrival. Later, a party led by Van Helsing and Mina reaches it at sunrise, and Mina's hypnotic trance points them along a road from the Pass.
An old-fashioned hotel in Bistritz where Harker stays and receives Count Dracula's letter.
Is English and an Anglican churchman who is wary of the crucifix he has been given.
An English traveller and narrator who keeps a shorthand journal, is practical and curious, and is uneasy about superstitions he encounters in Transylvania. He is an English Churchman by upbringing.

An English solicitor newly qualified and travelling in Transylvania on business for Mr. Hawkins. He is practical and uneasy about the strange household he has entered, keeping a careful journal of events.
Has been seriously ill with brain fever in a Buda-Pesth hospital, and has told the nurses he is engaged to Mina.
Has lost his memory of recent events after a shock and brain fever, and asks Mina never to learn what he wrote.
Partner in the firm of Hawkins & Harker, troubled by his nervous shock and the responsibility of his inheritance.
Has recovered from his shock and no longer fears the Count, after reading Van Helsing's letter confirming the truth of his journal.
Jonathan Harker is a clever, energetic, cool-headed man of great nerve, now collating evidence with his wife.
Left grey-haired and haggard by grief over Mina, though his energy remains strong.

Jonathan Harker is an English solicitor's clerk, a young man who travels to the Carpathians on business. He is courteous and careful, meeting the Count's hospitality with proper manners while noting the details of what he sees. He is also a practical man of affairs, handling the purchase of an estate and its legal papers, and he is wary of the crucifix he has been given.

Jonathan Harker is an English young man of affairs, a solicitor's clerk who travels abroad on business and is courteous, careful and observant. He handles estate purchases and legal papers, keeps a shorthand journal, and is engaged to Mina Murray. He is wary of the crucifix he has been given, and he has not written home for some time.

Jonathan Harker is an English young man of affairs and a solicitor's clerk, working in law at Exeter, who travels abroad on business. He is courteous and observant, keeps a shorthand journal, and is engaged to Mina Murray. He is wary of the crucifix he has been given, and he has been silent for some time, with no news of him reaching Mina.

Jonathan Harker is an English young man of affairs, a solicitor's clerk and partner in the Exeter firm of Hawkins & Harker, who travels abroad on business. He keeps a shorthand journal, is engaged to Mina Murray, and is courteous, observant and wary of the crucifix he was given. Since a serious illness and a shock he has lost his memory of recent events and has asked Mina never to learn what he wrote.

Jonathan Harker is an English solicitor's clerk and partner in the Exeter firm of Hawkins & Harker, engaged to Mina Murray. He is courteous and observant, keeps a shorthand journal, and once fell gravely ill abroad. Since a shock and brain fever he has lost his memory of recent events and asked Mina never to learn what he wrote, though he has since recovered and no longer fears the Count.

English solicitor and junior partner in the Exeter firm Hawkins & Harker, husband of Mina. Clever, energetic and cool-headed, a man of great nerve who keeps a journal. He was gravely ill abroad, leaving him weakened and prone to sudden waking fright, and he has lost his memory of recent events. He recovered from that shock and works alongside his wife, collating evidence.

English solicitor and junior partner in the Exeter firm Hawkins & Harker, husband of Mina. Clever, energetic and cool-headed, a man of great nerve who keeps a journal and works alongside his wife, collating evidence. Weakened by a long serious illness abroad that leaves him prone to sudden waking fright, and he has lost his memory of recent events. He has grown grey and haggard from grief, though his energy remains strong.
Hungarian name for a snowy mountain peak, meaning God's seat.
A poem whose line a passenger whispers, alluding to the dead riding fast.
The town where Mina and Jonathan Harker now live.

Peter Hawkins of Exeter, a solicitor who handles the Count's legal affairs and is a friend to both the Count and Jonathan Harker. Exeter is the city where Hawkins works, and the Count expects Harker to be there, miles away, working on legal papers with Hawkins. It is also marked on an atlas as one of the places ringed in England, alongside London and Whitby.

Peter Hawkins, a solicitor based in Exeter, a cathedral city far from London. He handles the Count's legal affairs, is a friend to both the Count and Jonathan Harker, and acts for the Count in buying his London estate. Exeter is where Hawkins works, and it is marked on an atlas as one of the ringed places in England, alongside London and Whitby.

Peter Hawkins, a solicitor in Exeter, a cathedral city far from London. He handles the Count's legal affairs and is a friend to both the Count and Jonathan Harker. Later passages show him dead, having left his estate to Jonathan and Mina Harker.

Exeter is a cathedral city far from London, home to the solicitor Peter Hawkins, who handles the Count's legal affairs and is a friend to Jonathan Harker. It is the town where Mina and Jonathan Harker live, where Jonathan works as a solicitor and partner. Peter Hawkins, dead and buried, left his estate to the Harkers.

Exeter is a cathedral city far from London, home to Mina and Jonathan Harker. Jonathan is a solicitor and partner in the town. Peter Hawkins, a solicitor and friend of Jonathan's, lived there; he is dead and buried, and his estate was left to the Harkers.

Peter Hawkins is a solicitor of Exeter who acts as an agent and legal representative for the Count in dealings in England. He is described as a friend of Jonathan Harker's and the Count's, and is the person to whom the Count's papers and letters concerning the London estate are sent. He also appears to be the sender of a letter the narrator delivers to the Count.

Peter Hawkins is a solicitor in Exeter, far from London, who acts as the Count's agent in English property and legal matters. He is a friend of both the Count and Jonathan Harker, and the Count's letters and papers concerning the London estate are directed to him. The Count also describes him as having bought the Purfleet property through the narrator.

Peter Hawkins is a solicitor in Exeter, far from London, and acts as the Count's agent in English property and legal affairs. He is a friend of Jonathan Harker, and the Count describes him as the one who bought the Purfleet estate through the narrator. Letters meant for Harker and Mina Murray pass through him, and Mina reports receiving news from Harker via Hawkins.

Dead: Mr. Hawkins has died suddenly, leaving his fortune to Jonathan and Mina Harker. A solicitor of Exeter, far from London, and the Count's agent in English property and legal affairs, he buys the Purfleet estate through the narrator. He is a friend of Jonathan Harker, takes him into partnership, and houses the couple, and his letters reach Mina.
A house near Purfleet, empty and in part ruined, with an old chapel forming part of it, where a consignment of boxes is to be deposited.

Carfax is a rundown estate on a by-road near Purfleet, with a large old house of many periods, a thick stone keep-like section, and an old chapel. It is enclosed by a high stone wall and contains about twenty acres, with trees and a dark pond. Its house is empty and for sale, and it is the place where fifty boxes are to be deposited.

Carfax is a walled estate on a by-road near Purfleet, once called Quatre Face for its four-sided house. It holds about twenty acres of trees and a dark pond, and includes a stone keep-like section beside an old chapel. The house is empty, and it is where a consignment of fifty boxes is to be delivered.

Carfax is a walled estate near Purfleet, once called Quatre Face for its four-sided house. It holds about twenty acres of trees and a dark pond, with a stone keep-like section beside an old chapel. The house stands empty, and it is where a consignment of fifty boxes is delivered.

Carfax is a walled estate near Purfleet, reached through old oak and iron gates, and it was once called Quatre Face for its four-sided house. It covers about twenty acres of trees and a dark pond, and holds a very old stone section beside a chapel. The house is largely empty and dusty, and fifty earth-filled boxes were delivered there.

Carfax is a walled estate near Purfleet, once called Quatre Face for its four-sided house, with about twenty acres of trees, a dark pond, and an old stone section beside a chapel. The house is very large and mostly empty and dusty, and fifty earth-filled boxes were delivered there. It is also the place from which boxes were later carried away to houses across London.

Whitby is a seaside town on the Yorkshire coast, marked on Count Dracula's atlas with a small ring beside Exeter and London. A letter addressed to Samuel F. Billington at No. 7, The Crescent, Whitby, is among the Count's outgoing post, so Billington is someone the Count writes to there.

Whitby is a seaside town on the Yorkshire coast, with a red-roofed old quarter above a harbour, a ruined abbey, and a churchyard on the cliff that people sit in to enjoy the view. On Count Dracula's atlas it is marked with a small ring beside Exeter and London. A letter addressed to Samuel F. Billington at No. 7, The Crescent, Whitby, is among the Count's outgoing post, so Billington is someone the Count writes to there. Mina Murray goes there to meet Lucy, who has rooms at a house on The Crescent.

A seaside town on the Yorkshire coast, with red-roofed houses above a harbour, a ruined abbey and a churchyard on the cliff where people sit to watch the sea. Count Dracula's atlas has a small ring marked on it, and he addresses a letter there to Samuel F. Billington at No. 7, The Crescent. Lucy Westenra and Mina Murray stay at a house on The Crescent; Mina arrives there to meet Lucy.

A seaside town on the Yorkshire coast, with red-roofed houses stacked above a harbour, a ruined abbey and a churchyard on the East Cliff where people sit to watch the sea. Samuel F. Billington, a solicitor, has an address at No. 7, The Crescent. Lucy Westenra and Mina Murray stay at a house on The Crescent, and a ring marked on an atlas in Count Dracula's study picks it out.
A London legal institution where Harker studied law.
A London bank to which Harker addresses one of his letters.
A recipient of one of Harker's letters, at Varna.

A recipient of a sealed letter written by Jonathan Harker, addressed to Herr Leutner at Varna; the letter is among those the Count stamps for posting. Beyond that, the passages say nothing more about who Herr Leutner is.
Bankers at Buda-Pesth to whom Harker addresses a letter.
A recipient of one of Harker's letters, living at The Crescent, Whitby.
A Whitby solicitor of 7, The Crescent, to whom the Demeter's cargo of wooden boxes is consigned, and who formally takes possession of the goods.

Samuel F. Billington is a Whitby solicitor living at 7, The Crescent. He is the consignee of the mould-filled wooden boxes aboard the Russian schooner Demeter, and he goes aboard to take formal possession of them. A letter from the Count is addressed to him, and he is described only through his business dealings.

A Whitby solicitor whose office is at 7, The Crescent, and who acts as consignee of the wooden boxes of mould shipped on the Russian schooner Demeter, formally taking possession of them. He trades as Samuel F. Billington & Son, and corresponds with London carriers on urgent shipments. A letter from the Count is addressed to him, and he is known only through these business dealings.

Varna is a port city, the place a Russian schooner, the Demeter, sailed from, and it is also where a banker, Herr Leutner, receives letters. It appears only as a location and a point of origin, with no described look, nature or manner.

Varna is a port city on the coast, the place from which the Russian schooner Demeter sailed, and where the banker Herr Leutner receives letters. The passages show it only as a location and point of origin, with no described look, nature or manner.

Varna is a port city on the coast, the origin of the Russian schooner Demeter and of the Czarina Catherine, both bound for Whitby and the Black Sea. Herr Leutner, a banker, is based there and receives letters from the Count's household. Consigned boxes are to be delivered to an agent there, and the Count's party plans to reach it overland ahead of the ship.

Varna is a Black Sea port city, a departure point for ships bound toward the Danube and Whitby. It is where the banker Herr Leutner is based and where the agent Ristics is to receive a consigned box. The travelling party reaches it by land, arriving ahead of the ship, and is waiting there for the Czarina Catherine to arrive.

Gipsies of Transylvania who attach themselves to a great noble and take his name. They are fearless, without religion beyond superstition, and speak their own Romany tongue. They are camped in the castle courtyard and are seen carrying out labour for the Count.

The Szgany are gipsies of the region, a band encamped in the castle courtyard who call themselves after their noble, and speak only their own Romany variety. Fearless and without religion beyond superstition, they serve the Count as workers and carriers, moving sealed boxes about the castle; their hetman leads them. They seem to take orders without asking questions.

Szgany are gipsies of the region, a band encamped in the castle courtyard who call themselves after their noble and speak only their own Romany variety. Fearless and without religion beyond superstition, they serve the Count as workers and carriers, moving sealed boxes about the castle and loading them onto leiter-wagons. Their hetman leads them, and they take orders without asking questions. They fight when cornered, and in a later encounter one band rides near a cart carrying a great box, with their leader giving commands to his men.
Two great wagons drawn by eight horses each, which bring heavy square boxes into the castle yard.
A distressed woman at the castle gate who calls the Count a monster and demands her child back.
An old chapel below the castle, used as a graveyard, reached through a stone passage and winding stair.
Dim underground vaults beneath the ruined chapel, holding old coffins and dust.
A young woman in London and Mina Murray's dearest friend since childhood. She is courted by several men and is in love with Arthur Holmwood.
Is a trifle stouter and rosy-cheeked, having lost her pale look at Whitby, and walks in her sleep.
Has grown pale and weak, and is sleepwalking and sometimes found at open windows; she is engaged to Arthur Holmwood.
Her condition is now critically weak, with ghastly pallor and failing breath, needing transfusions to survive.
Her mother Mrs. Westenra has died, and Lucy is now weakened, with wounds on her throat vanished at the end of her life.
Her death and burial are reported in a telegram, along with Mrs. Westenra's, as lost to the living.
Has become a vampire, with fresh blood on her lips and hellish eyes that show hatred toward those who knew her.
After being destroyed, her body is at rest as true dead, and her soul is said to be with God.

Lucy Westenra is a young woman who writes long, chatty letters to her close friend Mina Murray, sharing confidences about her day and her suitors. She is warm, playful and open-hearted, quick to laugh but also tender and quick to cry. Two men, Dr. Seward and Quincey P. Morris, have proposed to her, and she mentions being close to Arthur, whom she has been helping with his attentions. Her manner shows a lively, romantic temperament.

Lucy Westenra is a young woman who writes confiding letters to her close friend Mina Murray, and she is close with Arthur Holmwood, whom she has been helping in his attentions. Two men, Dr. Seward and Quincey P. Morris, have proposed to her. She is sweet and charming, especially with older people, and she sleepwalks. She has grown a trifle stouter with rosy cheeks, having lost the pale look she had before.

Lucy Westenra is a young woman, daughter of Mrs. Westenra and close friend of Mina Murray, who writes to her in confidence. She is sweet and charming, especially with old people, and sleepwalks, once waking in a churchyard at night. Her health has declined, and small wounds mark her throat, while Dr. Van Helsing and Dr. Seward watch over her closely.

Lucy Westenra is a young woman, daughter of Mrs. Westenra and close friend of Mina Murray, to whom she writes in confidence. She is sweet and charming, especially with old people, and her colour has returned since Whitby. Her health has declined, she walks in her sleep and is found faint at open windows, and small wounds on her throat do not heal, while Dr. Van Helsing and Dr. Seward watch over her closely. Arthur Holmwood, son of Lord Godalming, is her suitor.
A clever, resolute doctor of about twenty-nine who runs a large lunatic asylum. He proposes to Lucy Westenra and is refused.
Is a physician who has written to Van Helsing for help with Lucy's case, and who is bound to Arthur by friendship.
Follows Van Helsing's advice to tell his patients nothing of what he knows or thinks.
Doctor who travels to Hillingham to attend Lucy during her illness, working alongside Van Helsing.
Doubts Van Helsing's claims and suspects his mind may be unhinged, while still looking for a rational explanation.
Watches the horror at the tomb with a sinking heart after having rejected the proofs earlier.

Dr. John Seward is a doctor who runs a lunatic asylum and is a close friend of Quincey P. Morris and Arthur. He is a man of strong jaw and good forehead, outwardly cool but nervous in manner, and he proposes marriage to Lucy Westenra, who turns him down.

A physician who runs a lunatic asylum and keeps close friendship with Arthur and Quincey P. Morris. He has a strong jaw and good forehead, appears outwardly cool but is nervous, and has proposed marriage to Lucy Westenra, who refused him. He is also the one who writes to Van Helsing for help with Lucy's illness and keeps a diary of the case.

A physician who runs a lunatic asylum and keeps a diary of his cases. He is a close friend of Arthur Holmwood and Quincey P. Morris, outwardly cool yet inwardly nervous, with a strong jaw and good forehead. He once proposed marriage to Lucy Westenra, who refused him, and he works as her doctor alongside Van Helsing, following his advice to tell his patients nothing.

A physician who keeps a diary of his cases and runs a lunatic asylum, and who is a close friend of Arthur Holmwood. Outwardly cool but inwardly nervous, with a strong jaw and good forehead, he once proposed to Lucy Westenra and was refused. He works as her doctor alongside Van Helsing, whose advice to tell patients nothing he follows, and he treats Renfield as his most absorbing case. He doubts Van Helsing's claims while still seeking a rational explanation, and is worn by exhaustion and grief.

A physician who runs a lunatic asylum and is a close friend of Arthur Holmwood. Outwardly cool but inwardly nervous, with a strong jaw and good forehead, he once proposed to Lucy Westenra and was refused. He works as her doctor beside Van Helsing, whose advice he follows in telling patients nothing, and he doubts Van Helsing's claims while still seeking a rational explanation. He keeps a diary of his cases and is worn by exhaustion and grief.

A physician who runs a private asylum and is a close friend of Arthur Holmwood. Outwardly cool but inwardly nervous, he once proposed to Lucy Westenra and was refused. He attends Lucy as her doctor alongside Van Helsing, follows Van Helsing's advice to tell patients nothing, and keeps a diary of his cases. He doubts Van Helsing's claims while still seeking a rational explanation, and is worn down by exhaustion and grief.

A physician who runs a private asylum, a close friend of Arthur Holmwood, and a keeper of diaries. Outwardly cool but inwardly nervous and worn down, he once proposed to Lucy Westenra and was refused. He attends Lucy alongside Van Helsing, doubts Van Helsing's claims while still seeking a rational explanation, and takes part in the group's joint undertaking against the Count.
An American from Texas who speaks in slang to amuse Lucy but is well educated. He proposes to Lucy, is refused, and remains a friend.

Quincey P. Morris is an American from Texas, a well-mannered, cheerful man who looks young and fresh despite having travelled widely. He uses American slang mainly to amuse Lucy when no strangers are present, and is clearly nervous and sincere when he proposes to her. He is a close friend of Arthur Holmwood and of Jack Seward, and when Lucy declines him he accepts it with good grace and offers to remain a loyal friend.

Quincey P. Morris is an American from Texas, a close friend of Arthur Holmwood and Jack Seward, and a well-mannered, cheerful man who looks young and fresh despite his travels. He uses American slang mainly to amuse Lucy when no strangers are present, and he is nervous and sincere when he proposes to her. Once Lucy declines, he accepts it gracefully and offers to stay a loyal friend. He is steady in a crisis, offering blood for Lucy and standing ready to help.

Quincey P. Morris is an American from Texas, a well-mannered and cheerful man who looks young and fresh despite his many travels. He is close to Arthur Holmwood and Jack Seward, and once proposed to Lucy, accepting her refusal gracefully and offering to stay a loyal friend. He is steady in a crisis: he gives his blood for Lucy, keeps watch over the house, and bears Lucy's death with quiet courage.

Quincey P. Morris is an American from Texas, a well-mannered, cheerful man who looks young and fresh despite his many travels. He is a close friend of Arthur Holmwood and Jack Seward and once proposed to Lucy, accepting her refusal with grace. He is steady in a crisis: he gives his blood for Lucy, patrols the house through the night, and joins the vigil at the tomb.

An American from Texas, well-mannered and cheerful, who looks young and fresh despite his travels. A close friend of Arthur Holmwood and Jack Seward, and once a suitor of Lucy who accepted her refusal gracefully. Steady and brave in a crisis: he gives his blood for Lucy, patrols the house through the night, and joins the vigil at the tomb.

Quincey P. Morris is an American from Texas, cheerful, well-mannered and brave, who looks young and fresh. He is a close friend of Arthur Holmwood and Jack Seward, and once courted Lucy, accepting her refusal gracefully. In a crisis he is steady and reliable: he gives his blood for Lucy, patrols the house through the night, and joins the vigil at the tomb and the hunt that follows.
A patient of Dr. Seward's asylum, aged fifty-nine, sanguine and physically strong, prone to gloomy spells and fixed ideas.
Is a sanguine patient with a love of animals and a secret scheme; he keeps a note-book full of figures and collects living things.
Has a homicidal, life-devouring mania, and eats the living creatures he collects, which the doctor classes as zoöphagous.
Calms under the moon and speaks of waiting; his fits of violence recur at noon and sunset.
A patient of Dr. Seward's asylum who alternates between violent fits and quiet spells, and who collects and eats living creatures.

A patient of Dr. Seward's asylum who alternates between violent fits and quiet spells, and who collects and eats living creatures. He speaks of his master and is suspected of linking his outbursts to the Count.
Speaks with courtly, rational composure in this scene, claiming to have been once an inmate of a lunatic asylum.
Pleads desperately to be released, claiming he is sane and that he holds a secret he cannot reveal.
Called the Count 'lord and master' and is feared by Seward as a possible agent of the Count.
Speaks of himself as commanding destiny and says he wants life, not souls, with friends who will never let him lack the means of life.
Says he was sane apart from being unable to speak during the period when he begged to be let go, and hints at a secret he must reveal.
Describes the Count as a solid, fierce-eyed figure who came to his window, and says he admitted him to the room.
Claims to have attacked the Count to stop him drawing life from Mrs. Harker, believing madmen have unnatural strength.
Is devoted to Lucy and volunteers his own blood for her transfusion.

Hon. Arthur Holmwood, only son of Lord Godalming, and a frequent visitor to the Westenra household, where he gets on well with Mrs. Westenra. Lucy speaks of him with affection and refers to him by his first name, and a coming marriage is discussed in the passages. He corresponds with Quincey P. Morris, and is reported by letter and telegram as occupied with his ailing father.

Hon. Arthur Holmwood, the only son of Lord Godalming, is a frequent and welcome visitor to the Westenra household, where he gets on well with Mrs. Westenra. Lucy speaks of him with deep affection, and their coming marriage is discussed. He is often away from Whitby, called to see his ailing father, and he is described as tall and curly-haired.

Arthur Holmwood is a tall, curly-haired man who is the only son of Lord Godalming and is known with the courtesy title Hon. He is Lucy Westenra's intended husband and a frequent, welcome guest of the Westenra household, where he gets on well with her mother. He is often away, called to Ring to attend his gravely ill father. He keeps up correspondence with Quincey P. Morris and is also written to by Dr. Seward.

Hon. Arthur Holmwood, the only son of Lord Godalming and a tall, curly-haired man, is Lucy Westenra's intended husband. He is a frequent and welcome visitor to the Westenra household, and is often away, called to Ring to attend his gravely ill father. He keeps up correspondence with Quincey P. Morris and is also written to by Dr. Seward.

Son of Lord Godalming and engaged to Lucy Westenra, he is a tall, curly-haired gentleman who visits her household often. He is often called away to Ring to tend his gravely ill father. He offers his own blood to help save Lucy, and keeps up correspondence with Dr. Seward and Quincey P. Morris.

Arthur Holmwood, the Hon. Arthur, only son of Lord Godalming, and engaged to Lucy Westenra. A tall, curly-haired gentleman who often visits Lucy's household, and is repeatedly called away to Ring because his father is gravely ill. Devoted and open-hearted, he gives his own blood for Lucy's transfusion, is anxious for her, and is shaken at her changed, dying state, asking after her and pleading with the doctors.
A headland stretching out into the sea beyond Whitby harbour.

Kettleness is a headland that stretches out into the sea beyond Whitby's harbour, visible from the churchyard above the town. It is steep, with part of its bank having fallen away, and it is named in a gravestone inscription recording a man's fatal fall from its rocks. It appears here as a place and landmark, not as a person.

Kettleness is a steep headland stretching out into the sea beyond Whitby's harbour, seen from the churchyard above the town. Part of its bank has fallen away, and a gravestone names it as the place where a man fell to his death. It is a landmark in the scenery, not a person.
A large ruined abbey above Whitby, sacked by the Danes, with a legend of a white lady seen in a window.

An old, gnarled Whitby man who claims to be nearly a hundred and to have been a sailor in the Greenland fishing fleet. Sceptical of legends, he delights in gloomy talk about the dead and their tombstones.
Found dead on the churchyard seat in the morning, apparently having fallen back in fright, with a look of horror on his face.

Mr. Swales is an elderly local man of Whitby, a talkative, dialect-speaking old seaman who once sailed the northern seas. He is sharp-tongued and mocking toward the gravestones and their sentimental inscriptions, delighting in gruff jokes with his cronies. Later he approaches the narrator with a gentler manner.

Elderly local man of Whitby, a talkative old seaman in dialect who once sailed the northern seas. Sharp-tongued and mocking toward the gravestones and their sentimental inscriptions, he enjoys gruff jokes with his cronies. Later he approaches the narrator with a gentler manner, and he is found dead on the churchyard seat in the morning, apparently having fallen back in fright, with a look of horror on his face.
A master mariner named on a churchyard tombstone, said to have been murdered by pirates off Andres in 1854.
A man named on a churchyard tombstone at Kettleness, said by Mr. Swales to have taken his own life.

A man named in a gravestone inscription at Kettleness, described by a local fisherman as deformed and bitter toward his mother, who is said to have died by falling from the rocks after shooting himself. He is only known through others' accounts and the tombstone's claims.

Lord Godalming is the father of Arthur Holmwood, and is described as a close friend of Mrs. Westenra. He is ill at the time, and his son is called to his side at Ring. He does not appear in person in these passages; his standing is reported through others.

Lord Godalming is the father of Arthur Holmwood, the Hon. Arthur Holmwood, and a close friend of Mrs. Westenra. He is unwell and lives at Ring, where his son is summoned to attend him. In these passages he never appears in person; he is spoken of by others, who report he has been taken seriously ill. He is also said to have given Van Helsing permission to read Lucy's letters and papers.

Lord Godalming is the father of the Hon. Arthur Holmwood, and a long-standing friend of Mrs. Westenra. He is unwell and lives at Ring, where he has been taken seriously ill. Though spoken of often, he never appears in person, and he is said to have given Van Helsing permission to read Lucy's letters and papers.

Lord Godalming is the Hon. Arthur Holmwood's father, a long-standing friend of Mrs. Westenra and the late Lucy's fiancé's father. He is an elderly, unwell man who lives at Ring, where he was taken seriously ill, and he never appears in person. He is said to have given Van Helsing leave to read Lucy's letters and papers.

Lord Godalming is an elderly, unwell peer, father of the Hon. Arthur Holmwood and a long-standing friend of Mrs. Westenra. He is taken seriously ill at Ring and is never seen in person. He gave Van Helsing leave to read Lucy's letters and papers, and is called Arthur Holmwood's father in the passages.

Lord Godalming is the elderly father of the Hon. Arthur Holmwood, with his seat at Ring, and is known as Arthur's father. He has been seriously ill and is not seen in person, though he is spoken of as dear to the Westenra family. He is named as a friend of Mrs. Westenra and Lucy's family, and a man of loved and honoured standing. He gave Van Helsing leave to read Lucy's letters and papers.

Ring is a place where Mr. Holmwood is called to see his father, who has fallen seriously ill. Letters are sent there to him, so it is where he can be reached. The passages show nothing more about what it is like.
A coastguard at Whitby who keeps a spy-glass and talks with Mina.
A coastguard on duty on the eastern side of Whitby harbour, who is the first to climb aboard the Demeter and sees the dead steersman lashed to the wheel.
A high cliff at Whitby where a churchyard overlooks the sea and where a new searchlight is installed.

East Cliff is a high headland overlooking Whitby harbour, its churchyard and walk commanding a wide view of the sea to the north and east. Its summit holds a new searchlight, and the cliff-side churchyard hangs steeply over the lane to the East Pier. Locals watch weather signs from it, and a steep sand-heap at its foot is known as Tate Hill Pier.

East Cliff is a high headland above Whitby harbour, crowned by a churchyard with a walk and a new searchlight on its summit. Locals and holidaymakers gather there to watch the sea and weather, and it is a favourite spot where Lucy and the narrator sit. The cliff-side churchyard hangs steeply over the lane to the East Pier.
A small pier in Whitby harbour, on the south-east side, where the Demeter ran aground on a sand heap.

Tate Hill Pier is a small pier in Whitby harbour, on the south-east side of the harbour mouth beneath the East Cliff. It is a bank of sand and gravel where vessels can run aground, and it is close to the houses and the churchyard steps above, so people there are often first to reach a stranded ship.
A doctor of East Elliot Place, Whitby, who examined the dead steersman and judged he had been dead about two days.
A Russian schooner from Varna that drifts into Whitby harbour in a storm, carrying silver sand and boxes of earth, with a dead steersman lashed to her wheel.

Demeter is a Russian schooner out of Varna, found derelict in a storm off Whitby. It is almost entirely loaded with silver sand as ballast, carrying only a few wooden boxes of mould, and its captain is its commander.
A large dog belonging to a Whitby coal merchant, found dead with its throat torn out.
A Demeter crewman who relieved Petrofsky on watch.
A member of the Demeter's crew who goes missing during the voyage.
A Demeter crewman who reports seeing a tall, thin stranger aboard the ship.
A London carrying firm employed to deliver a consignment of boxes to Carfax, near Purfleet.

Carter, Paterson & Co. is a London firm of carriers that corresponds in writing, through its letters, with the Whitby solicitors Samuel F. Billington & Son. It replies courteously and businesslike, acknowledging a payment, returning an overplus cheque, and confirming goods were delivered as instructed, with keys left in the main hall.
A nursing sister at a hospital in Buda-Pesth who writes to Mina about Jonathan Harker's illness.

Sister Agatha is a nurse at the Hospital of St. Joseph and Ste. Mary in Buda-Pesth, where she cares for Jonathan Harker during his brain fever. She writes with warmth and sympathy, passing on Harker's messages and reassurances to Miss Wilhelmina Murray, and she is careful and protective about his recovery.

A nurse at the Hospital of St. Joseph and Ste. Mary in Buda-Pesth, a warm and devout Sister who is gentle and protective with her patients. She cares for Jonathan Harker during his brain fever and writes on his behalf to Mr. Peter Hawkins and to Miss Wilhelmina Murray, offering sympathy and blessings. She keeps the raving of the sick in confidence and is willing to arrange Harker's wedding to Miss Murray through the Superior.
A station on the railway from which Jonathan Harker boarded a train, shouting for a ticket home.
A statesman whose saying Dr. Seward quotes, cited as one who understood life.
The Westenra family home, where Lucy is ill and receives visitors.

Hillingham is the Westenra family home, where Lucy Westenra and her mother live. Lucy is ill there, and Arthur and Jack visit it while Van Helsing examines her. Mrs. Westenra is said to be in poor health.

Hillingham is the Westenra family home, where Lucy Westenra lives with her mother, Mrs. Westenra. Lucy is ill there, and Arthur and Jack visit while Van Helsing examines her and later stays nearby to watch over her. The house is described as a comfortable place with rooms for sitting up through the night.
The London hotel from which Arthur Holmwood writes to Dr. Seward.

Amsterdam is the city where Professor Van Helsing lives and works, and it is the place from which he travels to London. Van Helsing is an elderly scientist and metaphysician known for an iron nerve, unshakable resolve and a warm, sympathetic heart, and John Seward writes to him about Lucy Westenra's condition.

Amsterdam is the city where Professor Van Helsing lives and works, and the place he travels back to between his visits to London. He is an elderly scientist and metaphysician with an iron nerve, an unshakable resolve and a warm, sympathetic heart, and he is known for his expertise in obscure diseases. He is a former master of John Seward, who writes to him and sends him telegrams, and he sends telegrams to Seward from Amsterdam.

Professor Van Helsing lives and works in Amsterdam, the city he returns to between visits to London. He is an elderly scientist and metaphysician, known for expertise in obscure diseases and an iron nerve, and he is a former master of John Seward. Seward writes to him, and Van Helsing sends telegrams back from the city.
An Amsterdam physician and old master of Dr. Seward, who knows obscure diseases and is summoned to examine Lucy.
Keeps his theories to himself, speaks in riddles about husbandry, and insists on careful recording of every case detail.
Physician who, with Seward, forces entry into Hillingham and insists the blood transfusions and fight for Lucy's life continue.
Keeps his private reasons close, and speaks of a coming bitter time and of laughter that comes and goes.
Declares Jonathan's journal true, vouches for Jonathan's sound mind, and is deeply moved by Mina's trust and goodness.
Believes Lucy was bitten in a trance and is now Un-Dead, and says her face looks sweet, unlike other vampires.
Uses consecrated bread and garlic to bar the tomb and shows deep religious conviction in the Un-Dead's destruction.
Van Helsing has kept Jonathan Harker's and Mina's diaries and leaves them with Seward to study before they meet again.
Believes the vampire has ancient cunning and power over the elements and lesser creatures.
Holds that the vampire can be confined to his coffin, destroyed by a wild rose branch, a sacred bullet, a stake, or a severed head.
Leads the search, arming the party with crucifix, garlic, revolver, knife, lamps and a consecrated wafer against the Count.
Reminds the group that the Count dined heavily the previous night and is likely to sleep late.
Has studied the papers on the Count and believes his power and knowledge are growing; he means to stamp him out.
Traced the Count's escape to the Czarina Catherine by questioning dock workers and checking shipping records.
Reads and reasons about the Count's criminal nature, believing the group's larger minds can outmatch the Count's child-brain.
Insists on taking Mina into the enemy's country, arguing her hypnotic power can guide them to the Count's castle.

Abraham Van Helsing is a doctor of Amsterdam, a physician of obscure diseases and a former teacher of John Seward, whom he calls his friend. He is a philosopher, metaphysician and scientist with an iron nerve, a steady temper, an unshakable resolve and a kind, true heart. He can sound arbitrary and blunt, yet he is gentle and warm with young women, and he is called in to examine Lucy Westenra.

Abraham Van Helsing is a doctor of Amsterdam and the former teacher of John Seward, whom he calls his friend. He is a philosopher, metaphysician and scientist, with iron nerve, an unshakable resolve and a kind, true heart, yet he can sound arbitrary and stern. Gentle with young women, he examines Lucy Westenra and performs a blood transfusion for her, and he is known to speak in riddles and to guard his theories closely.

Dutch physician Abraham Van Helsing, a doctor from Amsterdam and former teacher of John Seward, who calls him a friend. He is learned, serious and sometimes stern, with iron nerve and a deep, tender care for Lucy; he keeps his theories to himself, speaks in riddles, and insists every case detail be recorded. He performs the blood transfusions on Lucy and takes charge of her nursing, watching her closely through the night.

Dutch physician from Amsterdam, a learned, stern and deeply tender man who was once a teacher of Dr. Seward and remains his friend. He keeps his theories private, speaks in riddles, and insists every detail be recorded. He arranges and performs the blood transfusions for Lucy and insists the fight for her life go on, and with Seward he forces entry into the Westenra house after the household cannot be roused. He is moved by Mina's trust and goodness and shows deep religious conviction, using consecrated bread and garlic against the Un-Dead.

Dutch physician from Amsterdam, a learned, stern and tender man and a former teacher of Dr. Seward, who remains his friend. He keeps his theories private and speaks in riddles, but insists every detail be recorded. He treats Lucy, arranges and gives blood transfusions, and uses garlic and a sacred wafer against the Un-Dead, showing deep religious conviction. He is moved by Mina's trust and goodness, and he has been keeping the diaries.

Dutch physician from Amsterdam and a former teacher of Dr. Seward, who remains his friend. A stern, tender and deeply religious man who speaks in riddles and keeps his theories private, yet insists on careful records. He arranges and gives blood transfusions to Lucy, guards her with garlic and a consecrated wafer, and is said to have studied the Count and believed his power growing. He keeps the diaries, is moved by Mina's trust, and speaks plainly of the Un-Dead as a thing to be destroyed.

Dutch physician from Amsterdam, a former teacher of Dr. Seward and still his friend. Stern, tender and deeply religious, he speaks in riddles and keeps his theories private while insisting on careful records. He arranges Lucy's transfusions and guards her with garlic and a consecrated wafer, and he is said to have studied the Count and believed his power growing. He treats the Un-Dead as a thing to be destroyed and leads the search for the Count's resting place.
A London hotel where Van Helsing asks to have rooms reserved for him.
A newspaper for which Dr. Seward pretends to write a descriptive article.
A London station where Dr. Seward meets Van Helsing on arrival.

Liverpool Street is a London railway station, the point where Van Helsing meets Dr. Seward and then departs from; Seward later takes his way to Paddington instead. Its role is as a place of arrival and departure rather than a character in its own right.
The town from which a boxful of garlic is sent to Lucy each day.

Haarlem is a town, not a person, and is where a supply of garlic is sent from, grown in glass-houses by a friend of Van Helsing's named Vanderpool. Van Helsing has the garlic brought from there by telegram, and Lucy later receives a box of it from Haarlem each day.
A character from a play, mentioned by Lucy as a comparison for herself.
The hotel where Van Helsing is staying in London.

The Berkeley is a hotel in Piccadilly, where Van Helsing stays and where the group is asked to meet him at ten o'clock. It is a place for meeting and rest rather than a character with abilities of its own.
The Berkeley is a hotel in Piccadilly where Van Helsing stays and where he meets Dr. Seward. It serves as a base for the group, with a carriage waiting there and a telegram delivered to Van Helsing.
A newspaper whose reporter interviews the zoo keeper about the escaped wolf.

The Pall Mall Gazette is a newspaper, and in these passages it appears as the paper printing a 18 September report on an escaped wolf. Its interviewer, sent out by it, uses the paper's name as a kind of key to open doors, and the name is what gets him attention from the people he approaches. Nothing else about the paper itself is shown yet.
Elderly keeper in the Zoological Gardens who looks after the wolves, living in a cottage with his wife.

Thomas Bilder is the elderly keeper of the wolf section at the Zoölogical Gardens, living in a cottage behind the elephant-house with his wife. He is hospitable, talkative and fond of banter, speaks in a rough London dialect, and offers confident theories about animals. He is shown caring tenderly for the wolf Bersicker when it returns hurt.

A grey wolf in the Zoological Gardens, one of three brought from Norway to Jamrach's and bought four years ago. He was normally well-behaved and never gave trouble, and he is later found in a penitent state after escaping.

Bersicker is a grey wolf kept at Jamrach's animal establishment, one of three brought from Norway and bought some four years before. Described by its keeper as well-behaved and rarely troublesome, it is attached to Mr. Bilder and lets him stroke its ears. It breaks out of its cage, is said by a gardener to have been seen loose in the Park, and later returns on its own, cut about the head.
A dealer from whom the zoo bought the wolves.
Thomas Bilder's wife, who lives with him at the Zoological Gardens.
The place from which Van Helsing sends a telegram to Dr. Seward.
A doctor in charge of the empty house next to the asylum, writing a report to Dr. Seward about Renfield's violent episodes.

Patrick Hennessey is a doctor who writes reports to John Seward, M. D., promising to telegraph him at once about any important matter. He signs his letters formally and is shown as a careful, dutiful correspondent in his professional role.
An attendant at the asylum who had a finger broken while restraining Renfield.

names.value: Harris & Sons, Moving and Shipment Company

facets.text: A moving and shipment firm in Soho that employs the two carriers who fought with Renfield.
A carrier employed by Harris & Sons who fought with Renfield at the empty house.

Jack Smollet is a carrier employed by Harris & Sons, a moving and shipment company, who lives in Great Walworth. He is one of two burly men who had a violent scuffle with the patient Renfield at an empty house beside the asylum grounds, and he later gave his name and address to the asylum's doctor.

Jack Smollet is a burly carrier employed by Harris & Sons, a moving and shipment company, living at Dudding's Rents in Great Walworth. He is one of the two men who scuffled with the patient Renfield at the empty house by the asylum grounds, and he gave his name and address to Dr. Seward's asylum. He shows no special abilities beyond great physical strength and a combative temper.

A burly carrier with great physical strength and a combative temper, working for Harris & Sons, a moving and shipment company, and living at Dudding's Rents in Great Walworth. He is one of two men who fought with the patient Renfield at the empty house by the asylum grounds, and he gave his name and address to Dr. Seward's asylum. He is a fellow mate with Thomas Snelling, whom he is described as being responsible for, and he is recalled as a decent, intelligent, reliable workman who keeps a notebook of delivery destinations.
A carrier employed by Harris & Sons who fought with Renfield at the empty house.

Thomas Snelling is one of two carrier men, employed by Harris & Sons Moving and Shipment Company, who fight with a patient at an asylum after their cart stops nearby. He is a burly, strong man who, with his companion Jack Smollet, struggled against three men before being subdued. He lives in Peter Farley's Row, Guide Court, Bethnal Green, and is named in the doctor's report as a witness to the incident.

Walworth is a district of London, a place where several of the men connected to the transport of the boxes live or are sought. Joseph Smollet, a carrier, is said to be found at home there, and a Mr. Bloxam is directed to Potter's Court in Walworth.
A solicitor from the firm Wholeman, Sons, Marquand & Lidderdale, who handles Mrs. Westenra's estate.
The solicitors' firm that handled Mrs. Westenra's affairs and her testamentary wishes.
President of the Incorporated Law Society, represented at Mr. Hawkins's funeral by a gentleman.

Sir John Paxton is the President of the Incorporated Law Society. He is seen only through a gentleman who represents him at a funeral service, so he does not appear in person. A John Paxton is also named among drowned sailors, which may or may not be the same man.
A shop in Piccadilly outside which Mina and Jonathan see a pretty girl in a carriage.
A London park from which the group watches the Piccadilly house while they wait.

Green Park is a shaded public park in London, a place where characters sit to rest or wait out of sight. It is where Jonathan falls asleep on Mina's shoulder after a frightening sighting, and later where Mina, Van Helsing and others wait within view of a house while locksmiths open its door.

Hampstead is a place: a London neighbourhood with a heath and a hill, described as fresh and lonely, near where Lucy lies in a family tomb. In the newspaper reports, Hampstead is the district where children go missing and are found injured in the throat, with the strays said to have been with a "bloofer lady".
The phrase children use for a woman who lured them away, which the press repeats.

A term children use, reported in the press, for a woman who supposedly lures young children away, especially at night. Her identity and nature are unknown: the children's accounts are unreliable and the phrase may have spread by imitation. Children missed at night show small throat wounds, and the police have been alerted.
A newspaper that reports the Hampstead children's disappearances and injuries.

The Westminster Gazette is a newspaper, here shown as the publisher of two reports from 25 September about children found hurt or missing around Hampstead Heath. Its items carry a headline style and a sensational tone, reporting wounds in children's throats and a claimed lure by a "bloofer lady." It is presented as the source of reports, not as a person.

The Westminster Gazette is a London newspaper that prints sensational reports, using bold headline styling and an urgent, lurid tone. In these passages it publishes accounts of children found hurt or missing near Hampstead Heath, with wounds in their throats and a claimed lure by a "bloofer lady." Characters read it as a source of news, and it is shown only as a publication, never as a person.

names.value: Shooter's Hill side of Hampstead Heath

facets.text: The open ground near Hampstead where children have been going missing and returning hurt.

Hampstead Heath is an open area of land where young children have been going missing, most often in the evenings. Children found there have small wounds in the throat, and many say a 'bloofer lady' lured them away. One child was found weak under a furze bush on its Shooter's Hill side, which is less frequented.
A London railway station that Van Helsing will reach by train from Exeter.

Paddington is a London railway terminus, named in the passages as a stop on train routes. It is where travellers from Exeter and nearby places are told they will arrive, and where a character is to be met at a set time.
A place from which Jonathan Harker telegraphs that he is leaving by train.
A scientist, now dead, whose work on hypnotism Dr. Seward accepts.
A long-lived figure from scripture, cited by Van Helsing as an example of unusual lifespan.
A man said to have lived one hundred and sixty-nine years, cited by Van Helsing.
A doctor at the North Hospital, a friend of Van Helsing and Seward, who treats the injured child.

Dr. Vincent is a physician at the North Hospital in London and a friend of Van Helsing, whom he knew from Amsterdam. He is practical and reasonable, inclined to explain the child's punctures as an animal bite, perhaps from a bat or a loose wolf. He treats the children's 'bloofer lady' talk lightly and advises the parents to keep watch.
An inn where Van Helsing and Seward dine before going to the churchyard.
An inn near Hampstead Heath where Van Helsing and Seward get a cab back to town.

Un-Dead is a vampire-like creature, a dead person who does not stay in the grave. It can be a sleeping form that lies still and looks peaceful, and it hunts the living for blood. Lucy has become one. It can summon a wolf and has the strength of twenty men, and it is cunning, able to slip past those who guard its resting place.

Un-Dead is a vampire-like creature, a dead person who will not stay in the grave, sleeping in a tomb by night and rising to prey on the living, especially children, by drawing their blood. It has the strength of twenty men, can summon a wolf, and is cunning enough to slip past guards and garlic seals. Its name is Lucy, a young woman who died a week earlier and was bitten while sleepwalking, so she is Un-Dead in a sweet, peaceful sleeping form.

Un-Dead is a vampire-like creature: a dead woman, Lucy, who will not stay in her grave. Bitten while sleepwalking, she rests peacefully by day in her tomb and rises at night to prey on children by drawing their blood. Her face is sweet when asleep, and her kind are said to have the strength of twenty men, to summon a wolf, and to be cunning enough to get past garlic and other protections. Her name is Lucy, and she is held as Un-Dead; she is not described as alive.
The churchyard where Lucy is buried, the site of the tomb they plan to open.
A plant the Un-Dead cannot bear, used to bar the tomb and to fill Lucy's mouth after death.
A charred, pointed wooden stake that is driven through Lucy's heart to destroy her.
Consecrated bread that Van Helsing brought from Amsterdam and uses to seal the tomb against the Un-Dead.

The Host is a consecrated wafer that Van Helsing brought from Amsterdam and carries with him as a sacred object. He uses it as a holy instrument against the dead, placing pieces in the graves' earth so that the ground becomes sanctified.
A prayer book that Van Helsing reads from during the burial rite.

Telegram is a means of sending messages, used in the story as a form of written communication sent between characters. It appears as a message bearing a sender's name and a recipient's name, such as messages passing between Seward, Van Helsing, Holmwood and Mrs. Harker. Its content is given as short wire-style notes, some marked with dates and places.
A London station the train runs into on the way back to the city.

Fenchurch Street is a place in London, reached by Underground, where a lunatic asylum stands. Mrs. Harker is taken there, and it is the spot from which Lord Godalming and Quincey set out to find a locksmith before breaking into an empty house.
The typewriter Van Helsing and the others use to copy diaries and records into typed, ordered documents.
A recording device on which Dr. Seward keeps his spoken diary in cylinders.
The London carrying firm whose men delivered the boxes of earth to Carfax, with its own day-book and letter-book.

A London carrying firm whose central office and King's Cross branch handled the delivery of a consignment of boxes. Its staff keep day-books and way-bills, and its teaming men did the actual hauling to Carfax.
A London railway station where the boxes from Whitby were received and checked against the invoice.
A scholar at Buda-Pesth University whom Van Helsing asked to trace the history of Dracula.
A southern London district where another of the Count's houses and earth-lairs are thought to lie.

Bermondsey is a district south of the river, named as the location of a house the Count bought and where one of the earth-boxes was delivered. Jamaica Lane, Bermondsey, is the address given for six boxes, and deeds for a Bermondsey house are among the papers found at Carfax. It is a place to be searched and cleared of the boxes.

Bermondsey is a district south of the river where the Count acquired a house. Six earth-boxes were delivered to Jamaica Lane there, and deeds for Bermondsey and Mile End houses are among the papers found at Carfax. It is a place the group plans to visit and clear of the boxes.
An eastern London district where one of the Count's houses and earth-lairs are thought to lie.

Mile End is a district of East London where the group searches for the Count's earth-filled boxes, and where he has bought a house. Chicksand Street, Mile End New Town is a place where one cartload of boxes was left, and a deed for a house there is among the Count's papers. Lord Godalming and Quincey Morris are assigned to go there and destroy the lairs.
A carter who once moved boxes from Carfax for an old man, named by Smollet as someone who can say more.

Sam Bloxam is a rough-spoken, hard-drinking workman, a labourer on a cold-storage building site at Poplar. He is a smart enough fellow, and was once hired to carry heavy boxes between Carfax and a house in Piccadilly. He lodges at Corcoran's house in Walworth.
A street in Poplar where a new cold storage building is being erected.
House agents in Sackville Street who sold the Piccadilly house and guard their clients' affairs closely.
A house in Piccadilly, bought by the Count, where the group breaks in to search for his effects and his earth-boxes.

Piccadilly house is a large, empty mansion on Piccadilly, put up for sale and since sold, with its purchaser unnamed by the agents. It is linked to the house Dracula uses, holding eight of his nine earth-filled boxes, and it still smells strongly of him. Its title deeds lie among his effects in the dining-room.
An empty house near the Junior Constitutional in Piccadilly, one of the lairs where boxes were delivered.
A late owner of the Piccadilly house whose executors sold it.
A foreign nobleman who bought the Piccadilly house in notes over the counter, a name used by the purchaser.
An attendant at Dr. Seward's asylum who answers the alarm at Renfield's room and is sent away when Van Helsing operates. Careful and observant, he is puzzled by the injuries.
A death's-head moth, named by Van Helsing as a comparison for the moths Renfield describes.
A street near the Piccadilly house, where the group leaves their cab.
A sailing ship bound for Varna and the Black Sea, the vessel on which the Count's box is being shipped away from London.
A ship bound for Varna, believed to be carrying the Count in a box.

The Czarina Catherine is a merchant sailing ship that leaves the Thames for Varna and the Black Sea, and the travellers suspect Count Dracula has taken passage aboard her. Its captain is short-tempered and profane, and the vessel is said to be carrying a large box that a tall, pale man had loaded.

A merchant sailing ship bound from London to Varna and onward up the Danube, carrying a large box believed to hold Count Dracula. Its captain is loud and profane, and the ship is said to have been fogged in briefly when a tall, pale stranger came aboard to check on the box. By the latest telegrams it has been reported at the Dardanelles and has entered Galatz, while the travellers wait at Varna for its arrival.

A merchant sailing ship, the Czarina Catherine, carrying the box believed to hold the Count. Its captain is loud and profane, and it is said to have been fogged in when a tall, pale stranger came aboard to see the box. Reported at the Dardanelles, it has entered Galatz, where the box was cleared and handed to an agent.
A London wharf from which the Czarina Catherine sails for Varna.
The shipping register where the party looked up which vessels sailed for the Black Sea.
An agent at Varna to whom the box is to be given, who will present his credentials there.
A place where Morris and Harker were once chased by a pack of wolves.
A town where the Czarina Catherine is reported arriving, reached by a train the party must catch.

Galatz is a river port on the Danube, where a ship carrying the Count is reported to have arrived, and a train from Varna is set to reach it the next morning. It is a place, not a person, and its role is as the destination the travellers pursue.

Galatz is a river port on the Danube, the place where the ship carrying the Count arrives and where a box marked for him is cleared and handed on. It is a destination rather than a person, and the travellers rush toward it by train, hoping to intercept what has arrived there.
A figure of ancient learning quoted by Van Helsing on the power of a fulcrum.
A writer on criminal types whose classification Mina cites when describing the Count.
A writer on criminal types whose classification Mina cites when describing the Count.
Captain of the Czarina Catherine, a superstitious and canny Scot who ran the ship from London to Galatz.
A London firm whose agents at Galatz assisted the party.
Agents at Galatz for the London firm of Hapgood, who showed the party civility and took them aboard the ship.
The address of Immanuel Hildesheim's office at Galatz.
A Galatz agent who received the Count's box from the Czarina Catherine and passed it to Skinsky, paid by English banknote.

A Hebrew businessman with an office at Burgen-strasse 16 in Galatz, of a sheep-like nose and a fez, who handles cargo for a fee. He was hired to receive a box from the Czarina Catherine before sunrise and hand it to Petrof Skinsky, and he did so. He is paid in banknotes and gold, and is an unscrupulous go-between.
A Slovak trader on the river at Galatz, given the box by Hildesheim, later found murdered at St. Peter's churchyard.

Petrof Skinsky is a dealer who trades with the Slovaks shipping goods down the river to the port of Galatz. He receives a box from Immanuel Hildesheim and is said to have been found dead, his throat torn open, though the passages show only rumour of how he died, not who did it. He had a rented house and left town two days before the body was reported.
A river near Galatz, a possible route for the box, more easily navigated than the Sereth.

Pruth is a river, one of two candidates considered as the route a boxed cargo was carried up toward a castle. It is described as more easily navigated than the Sereth, and a reader is told only that it may be the waterway in question, not that it was used.
A river near Galatz, suspected as the waterway the box travelled up toward the Count's castle.
A river joining the Sereth at Fundu, running up round the Borgo Pass near the Count's castle.

Bistritza is a river in the Carpathian region, a tributary that joins the Sereth at Fundu and runs up round the Borgo Pass. The travellers follow it by steam launch and horse in pursuit of the Count, and its rapids are hard to climb.
A place where the Bistritza joins the Sereth, where the party gets a Roumanian flag and hears news of the boat.

Fundu is a place where the Sereth river meets the Bistritza, on the water route the travellers follow. Its boatmen and people are the source of news about the launch and other boats, and the travellers hoist a Roumanian flag there. It is said to be near the Borgo Pass.
A town where Mina and Van Helsing are to hire a carriage and horses for the drive to the Borgo Pass.

Veresti is a town in the region the travellers pass through, where they stop at noon to buy a carriage and horses and to gather provisions before setting out toward the Borgo Pass. It is the last settled place they reach before the country grows wild and houses become few. Its landlady prepares their supplies.
A place further up the river the party hopes to reach before needing to confer.

Grosset & Dunlap is a publisher whose name appears in advertising and back-matter, where its selected list of books is presented as an index of good fiction and a standard of value. It is also the house that issues the detective novels of J. S. Fletcher, and readers are told to ask for its list when buying them.

events.summary: Harker arrives at the Golden Krone Hotel in Bistritz and receives a letter from Count Dracula welcoming him and arranging his journey.
The landlord and his wife refuse to say anything about Count Dracula or his castle, and seem frightened.
The old landlady begs Harker not to go, then gives him a crucifix, which he wears despite his misgivings.
The villagers make the sign of the cross against the evil eye as the coach leaves Bistritz.
The coach driver says no carriage awaits Harker, but a black calèche driven by a tall bearded man arrives and takes him.
Harker leaves the coach and is driven into the Borgo Pass in the calèche, while the other passengers cross themselves.
The driver stops to investigate blue flames on the road, and wolves gather around the carriage.
The driver drives the wolves back with a sweep of his arms, and the carriage continues.
The carriage arrives at a vast ruined castle with no lights in its windows.
The driver leaves Harker alone at the castle gate and drives away with the calèche into the courtyard's dark passages.
The Count greets Harker, introduces himself as Dracula, and carries Harker's luggage up to a prepared bedroom.
The Count explains through the letter that he is ill with gout and will send a young servant instead to assist Harker.
Harker is repulsed by the Count's breath and touch and notices the howling of wolves from the valley.
Harker finds the castle richly furnished but without mirrors or bells, and discovers that the castle's doors are locked.
The Count tells Harker he may go anywhere except locked rooms, and says Transylvania's ways are strange to an Englishman.
The Count explains the blue flames as signs of hidden treasure buried in the blood-soaked ground of the region.
Harker and the Count go through the papers for the purchase of the Carfax estate at Purfleet, and Harker reads his notes on it.
Harker notices that an atlas has rings marked near London, Exeter and Whitby, and the Count's new estate lies near London.
Harker cuts himself shaving, and the Count reacts with fury at the blood until he touches the crucifix at Harker's neck.
The Count throws the shaving glass out of the window, shattering it, and withdraws without a word.
Harker discovers that every door in the castle is locked and realises he is a prisoner.
Harker realises he is a prisoner and decides to conceal his fears and knowledge from the Count.
Harker notices the Count does the household tasks himself and concludes the Count may have driven the coach that brought him.
Harker talks with the Count about Transylvanian history, and the Count speaks proudly of his race and ancestors.
The Count questions Harker about English legal procedure, consignments and agents for property and shipping.
The Count insists Harker stay a month longer and orders him to write letters saying so.
The Count hands Harker thin paper and envelopes, implying his letters will be read, so Harker plans to write formal notes and send secret letters in shorthand.
Harker secretly reads the Count's unsealed letters addressed to Herren Klopstock & Billreuth and Samuel Billington, then the Count returns and takes them.
The Count warns Harker never to sleep anywhere in the castle except his own chamber or the Count's rooms.
Harker places the crucifix above his bed to protect his sleep.
Harker sees the Count climb head-first down the castle wall, which horrifies him and makes him fear for his sanity.
