Harker falls asleep on a couch in the old ladies' room, against the Count's warning.
Three women appear in the moonlight, cast no shadows, and gather over Harker, who feels both longing and fear.
The Count bursts in, furiously stops the fair woman from biting Harker and commands the women to keep away from him.
The Count tells the women that Harker belongs to him and promises they may kiss him later.
The Count gives the women a struggling bag and they vanish through the window, after which Harker faints.
Has an uncanny ability to grow younger and bloated with blood after feeding, appearing full of fresh blood.
Under pressure, Harker writes three letters at the Count's request, dating them to be sent later, and realises he may not survive past the final date.
Harker's letter to the Count's rival or an unknown contact is burned in the lamp's flame.
The Count locks Harker in the study and later in his room, leaving him a prisoner.
Harker finds all his paper, notes, travel papers and letter of credit missing, and his travelling suit and overcoat gone.
Harker sees boxes delivered by wagons and realises he is locked in his room, unable to attract the drivers' attention.
Harker sees the Count leave by the window in Harker's own clothes, carrying a bag, planning to be seen as Harker.
Harker is hypnotised by the moonbeams and the three women begin to take shape, forcing him to flee to his room.
Harker climbs down the castle wall into the Count's room and finds the gold hoard and a stairway leading down.
Harker discovers the Count lying apparently dead in a box of earth in the ruined chapel.
The Count announces Harker will leave the next day and the Szgany and Slovaks will arrive to finish their work.
Harker reaches the great door, it is unlocked, and the Count opens it so wolves can come in; Harker begs him to shut it.
Through the door, Harker hears the Count tell the three women to wait, and sees them lick their lips before they run.
Harker finds the main door locked again after he left the Count, so he cannot leave.
Harker climbs back to the Count's room and goes down to the chapel to search for the key.
Harker raises a shovel to strike the Count, but the Count's eyes turn on him and the blow only gashes the forehead; the lid falls shut.
The Szgany and Slovaks arrive and the Count's door is locked behind Harker; Harker is trapped in the Count's room as the boxes are sealed.
The boxes are nailed shut and carried out; the wagons leave with their freight, and Harker is left alone in the castle with the women.
Harker resolves to climb the castle wall to escape, taking some gold with him.
Lucy writes to Mina that she loves Arthur Holmwood, though he has not yet declared himself.
Lucy receives her first proposal from Dr. John Seward, which she refuses, telling him there is someone else she cares for.
Quincey P. Morris proposes to Lucy, and she refuses him, telling him she loves another man.
Dr. Seward questions Renfield closely about his delusion, pressing him toward his madness in a way he later sees as cruel.
Quincey P. Morris invites Arthur Holmwood and Dr. Seward to a camp-fire gathering, and Arthur accepts by telegram.
Mina arrives in Whitby and Lucy meets her at the station, showing her the town and churchyard above the harbour.
Mr. Swales, an old sailor, scornfully dismisses the legends of the sea bells and the White Lady to Mina.
Mr. Swales and his cronies talk at length about tombstones, which he says are full of lies, and the sea-dead lost abroad.
At Mr. Swales's urging, Mina reads a tombstone for Edward Spencelagh, who was supposedly murdered by pirates off Andres.
Lucy tells Mina of her coming marriage to Arthur, and Mina admits she has had no letter from Jonathan for a month.
Dr. Seward notes Renfield's secretive purpose and his fly-catching, which Renfield insists on doing thoroughly.
Renfield eats a blow-fly he has caught, arguing that the life in it is good and wholesome.
Renfield has built a colony of sparrows and asks Seward for a kitten, which Seward refuses.
Renfield's sparrows have vanished, leaving feathers and blood; the attendant reports that he vomited feathers, suggesting he ate them.
Seward gives Renfield an opiate, reads his note-book and concludes he is a life-devouring maniac, planning to absorb lives step by step.
Mina receives a short letter from Jonathan dated from Castle Dracula, saying he is starting for home, which troubles her.
Mina and Mrs. Westenra agree that Mina will lock the door at night because Lucy has resumed sleepwalking.
Arthur Holmwood is called to Ring because his father is seriously ill, postponing his visit to Lucy.
Lucy wanders at night, searching the room for the key, and seems to be watching Mina even in sleep.
Mina hears no more from Jonathan; a storm threatens, and a Russian ship is seen behaving erratically off Whitby.
Mr. Swales confides that he fears death is near and apologises for his earlier mockery, then leaves Mina.
A sudden storm is foretold as a bank of mares'-tails appears in the north-west, and a foreign schooner is seen with sails set near the coast.
A searchlight picks out the schooner, which runs with sails set into the harbour and grounds on a sand heap at Tate Hill Pier, with a corpse lashed to her helm.
The coastguard boards first, finds the steersman tied to the wheel, and the correspondent and a doctor follow; the body is later removed to the mortuary.
Mr. Billington takes formal possession of the cargo and the Russian consul takes possession of the ship, while the dog vanishes and a mastiff is found dead.
The captain reports that the mate has gone mad and is searching the cargo boxes, and that the steersman has been found missing.
The mate, terrified, throws himself into the sea, and the captain prepares to bind himself to the wheel.
The inquest returns an open verdict, and the town plans a public funeral for the captain, with boats following his body up the Esk to the churchyard.
Lucy sleepwalks again, dressing herself twice, and Mina manages to undress her and return her to bed.
Mina and Lucy go to the harbour in the morning, and Mina grows anxious about Jonathan's whereabouts.
At the captain's funeral the dog of a quiet local man refuses to join its master and is thrown onto a tombstone, where it cowers in terror.
Mr. Swales is found dead on the churchyard seat with a look of fear on his face.
Mina decides to take Lucy on a long walk to Robin Hood's Bay and back so she will be too tired to sleepwalk.
Has escaped into the grounds of Carfax, speaking to an unseen master and declaring himself a slave, and is now chained in a padded room.
Lucy's mother confides to Mina that her heart is failing and she may die within months, and Mina promises to keep it secret.
Arthur's father recovers, and Arthur and Lucy's marriage is set to go ahead soon.
Lucy grows weaker, is found fainted at the open window, and the small wounds on her throat do not heal.
Solicitors Samuel F. Billington & Son instruct Carter, Paterson & Co. to deliver fifty boxes to Carfax, and the goods are duly deposited there.
Lucy recalls a dreamlike experience of floating above the lighthouse and of sinking into water, and laughs at it.
Mina receives news that Jonathan Harker has been ill and resolves to travel to him in Buda-Pesth to nurse him and bring him home.
Sister Agatha writes that Jonathan has been ill for six weeks and has told the staff of his engagement to Mina.
Renfield grows excited and haughty, declaring the Master is at hand and that the attendants no longer count.
Renfield escapes through a window, and Seward follows him to the walls of Carfax.
Renfield is overpowered after a violent struggle and chained in a padded room, where he speaks of waiting for the Master.
Mina and Jonathan are married in Buda-Pesth, and Jonathan gives her his secret book, which she seals under her wedding ring.
Renfield grows quiet at moonrise and asks to be relieved of restraint, and Dr. Seward agrees.
Renfield escapes again to the old chapel grounds, where a bat is seen flying west, and then goes quietly back.
Arthur Holmwood asks Dr. Seward to examine Lucy, whose doctor-diagnosed heart condition her mother has privately confided.
Dr. Seward finds Lucy's blood normal but suspects a mental cause, and summons Van Helsing.
Van Helsing agrees to come to London at once to help Lucy.
Van Helsing examines Lucy and finds no functional cause but insists there must be one, promising to return if needed.
Renfield has a violent outburst at noon and then sinks into melancholy.
At sunset Renfield has another fit, then calms, releases his flies and says he is sick of the rubbish.
Dr. Seward telegraphs Van Helsing that Lucy has taken a terrible turn for the worse and urges him to come at once.
Van Helsing arrives in London and meets Dr. Seward, who has not yet told Arthur the full truth about Lucy.
Van Helsing advises Dr. Seward to keep their knowledge to themselves and not reveal it to Arthur.
Van Helsing judges Lucy in mortal danger from blood loss and decides a blood transfusion must be given at once.
Arthur arrives unexpectedly at the house and offers himself to save Lucy, and Van Helsing accepts him as the donor.
Van Helsing performs the transfusion using Arthur's blood, restoring some of Lucy's strength.
Van Helsing notices a red mark on Lucy's throat beneath her velvet band and reacts in a way that betrays alarm.
Dr. Seward examines the mark and finds two small punctures over the vein, which he cannot explain.
Van Helsing leaves for Amsterdam, ordering Dr. Seward to watch Lucy all night and promising to return.
Dr. Seward sits up with Lucy, who sleeps peacefully after he promises to wake her if bad dreams come.
Van Helsing telegraphs that he is returning and asks Dr. Seward to be at Hillingham that night.
Lucy insists Dr. Seward rest and sleep in a nearby room while she keeps watch over herself.
Dr. Seward wakes to find Van Helsing at Lucy's bedside and they go in to check on her.
Lucy is found nearly dead, white and unconscious, with her gums shrunken, and the two doctors revive her with brandy.
Van Helsing gives Dr. Seward a second transfusion and a morphia injection to keep Lucy asleep.
Van Helsing warns Dr. Seward to say nothing of the transfusion to Arthur, lest he be frightened or jealous.
Van Helsing sends Dr. Seward home to rest, insisting he will sit up with Lucy himself and that the case must be kept secret.
Van Helsing receives a parcel of garlic flowers and places them around Lucy's room and round her neck as a protection.
Van Helsing rebukes Lucy sharply when she mocks the garlic, then gently assures her, and seals the windows with the flowers.
Returns to the zoo keeper's care on his own, with his head cut and full of broken glass from a wall.
Insists on performing the blood transfusion himself on the morning of 13 September and orders Dr. Seward to rest.
Dr. Seward and Van Helsing arrive at Hillingham and learn from Mrs. Westenra that Lucy is sleeping and better.
Mrs. Westenra reveals she removed the garlic flowers from Lucy's room and opened the window, which horrifies Van Helsing.
Van Helsing breaks down in despair, then resolves to act, and he and Dr. Seward go up to Lucy's room.
Dr. Seward gives Lucy another blood transfusion, with Van Helsing supplying the blood and ordering Dr. Seward to rest.
Van Helsing tells Mrs. Westenra the flowers have medicinal value and must not be moved, and takes over Lucy's care for two nights.
Lucy recovers over four days, her nightmares ceasing while Van Helsing is with her, and Van Helsing leaves for a day in Amsterdam.
The reporter interviews Thomas Bilder, the zoo keeper, who describes the wolf Bersicker escaping after a tall stranger with red eyes provoked him.
Bilder predicts the wolf is hiding nearby, then Bersicker is seen returning and is taken back into his cage.
A patient attacks Dr. Seward with a dinner-knife, cutting his wrist, and is subdued while licking up the spilled blood.
Van Helsing telegraphs Dr. Seward to be at Hillingham that night and to ensure the flowers are placed correctly, but the telegram arrives twenty-two hours late.
Mrs. Westenra comes to Lucy's room and lies down with her, and the flapping at the window begins again.
A large grey wolf breaks through the window and Mrs. Westenra dies of fright, and Lucy loses consciousness as a swarm of specks fills the room.
Lucy finds the maids drugged with laudanum and the mother's medicine bottle empty, leaving her alone with her mother's body.
Lucy writes a memorandum, hides it in her breast, and bids farewell to Arthur as she feels she may not survive the night.
Dr. Seward arrives at Hillingham early and finds the house silent and unresponsive, fearing Lucy may have died.
Van Helsing and Seward break into the house through a kitchen window and find the servants drugged and Lucy and her dead mother upstairs.
Van Helsing finds Lucy still alive and orders brandy, and the doctors begin reviving her.
Seward wakes the maids and orders a bath and hot fires, and they carry Lucy into the bath to warm her.
Quincey Morris appears, having been sent by Arthur, and offers his blood for another transfusion.
Van Helsing gives Lucy a further transfusion using Quincey's blood and a morphia injection, and she falls into deep sleep.
A sheet of note-paper that fell from Lucy's breast is read by Van Helsing and Seward, and Van Helsing says it will be explained later.
Seward proposes to fill in a death certificate attributing Mrs. Westenra's death to heart disease to avoid an inquest.
Quincey asks Seward whether Arthur was the first to give blood, and Seward confirms the transfusions have been going on for about ten days.
Quincey offers to help, and Seward says the doctors will stay with Lucy until she recovers or dies.
Lucy wakes, weeps for her mother, and in her sleep tears up the paper Van Helsing had given Seward.
Arthur arrives at Hillingham and speaks with Lucy, who rallies briefly in his presence.
Seward records his despair at the deaths of Mrs. Westenra, Mr. Hawkins and the threat hanging over Lucy.
Seward relieves Van Helsing at Lucy's bedside and sends Arthur to rest with Van Helsing.
At dawn Van Helsing examines Lucy's throat and finds the wounds have disappeared, and he declares she is dying.
Seward wakes Arthur, who kneels and weeps, and then they return to Lucy's room.
Lucy, in a voluptuous voice, calls for Arthur to kiss her, but Van Helsing pulls him back in fury, making him stand between them.
Lucy asks Van Helsing to guard Arthur and give her peace, and he solemnly swears to do so.
Lucy's breathing ceases, and Van Helsing declares her dead, though he says it is only the beginning.
The funeral is arranged for the next day so Lucy and her mother can be buried together, and Seward handles the formalities.
Van Helsing and Seward go through the papers, and Van Helsing takes Lucy's papers and the memorandum from her breast to examine privately.
Seward writes to Mrs. Westenra's solicitor after finding his name and address among her papers.
Van Helsing places wild garlic around Lucy's bed and a gold crucifix over her mouth.
Van Helsing reveals he wants to perform a post-mortem, cutting off Lucy's head and removing her heart, and asks Seward to help without telling anyone.
Van Helsing asks Seward for faith in him, and Seward promises it.
Van Helsing reveals the gold crucifix was stolen overnight and that he has recovered it from the woman who took it, and says the thief's punishment will come.
The solicitor Mr. Marquand explains that Mrs. Westenra left her whole estate to Arthur Holmwood, except one entailed property that goes to a distant branch of the family.
Arthur visits the death-chamber and breaks down in Seward's arms, then sees Lucy's face and kisses her hand and forehead before leaving.
Arthur accepts Van Helsing's request to keep Lucy's papers and letters, which Van Helsing will hold until the right time.
Van Helsing keeps watch over the house all night while Seward sleeps on a sofa in Arthur's room.
In Piccadilly Jonathan spots a tall, thin, dark man who he believes is the Count, though younger, and watches him follow a carriage away.
Mina and Jonathan return home to a telegram from Van Helsing reporting that Mrs. Westenra and Lucy have both died and been buried.
Arthur returns to Ring with Quincey Morris after the burial, and Van Helsing leaves for Amsterdam, planning to return to stay with Seward.
Van Helsing breaks into laughter and tears on the train with Seward and explains his mirth as King Laugh arriving unbidden.
Jonathan goes away for the day for work, and Mina decides to read his foreign journal.
Mina reads Jonathan's journal and resolves to prepare a typed copy in case others need to see it.
Van Helsing writes to Mina asking to see her, to read Lucy's letters and papers for matters of great importance.
Mina telegraphs Van Helsing inviting him to come that day.
Van Helsing visits Mina, who gives him her typed account of Lucy's sleepwalking and the shorthand diary.
Overwhelmed, Mina tells Van Helsing that Jonathan had a shock and that she fears the cause of his brain fever.
Mina gives Van Helsing a typed copy of Jonathan's journal, and he promises to visit the next morning.
Van Helsing writes that Jonathan's journal is true and that Jonathan's mind and heart are sound.
Mina writes to Van Helsing, inviting him to breakfast instead of lunch, as Jonathan is returning that night.
Jonathan returns and tells Mina his doubts are gone now that Van Helsing has confirmed his journal.
Van Helsing and Jonathan meet and shake hands, and Van Helsing asks Jonathan to tell him about his time before Transylvania.
At the station, Van Helsing reads the Westminster Gazette and turns pale, saying the matter has come so soon.
Van Helsing returns to Seward with a Westminster Gazette report of children with punctured throats at Hampstead, saying he has learned much.
Van Helsing argues that the throat wounds were made by Lucy herself, which Seward finds hard to accept.
Van Helsing confesses to Seward that Lucy is Un-Dead, and Seward is stunned and angry at the news.
Van Helsing proposes they visit the injured child at the hospital and then spend the night at Lucy's tomb.
Dr. Vincent shows the child's throat punctures, which resemble Lucy's, and suggests an animal or bat caused them.
Van Helsing opens the coffin and finds it empty, and then locks the tomb and gives Seward the key.
Van Helsing returns from the churchyard carrying a child with no throat wound, and the two men take it to the Heath for the police to find.
Arthur, Quincey and Seward meet Van Helsing, who asks them to promise to join him at the churchyard.
Van Helsing asks Arthur to promise to come, and Arthur insists on protecting Lucy's grave from outrage.
Arthur agrees to go with Van Helsing to the churchyard and wait, despite his anguish.
Arthur opens Lucy's coffin and finds the lead inner coffin rent open.
The coffin is found empty, astonishing the company.
Van Helsing seals the tomb with consecrated host and garlic to keep the Un-Dead out.
Lucy appears in the churchyard carrying a child, then drops it and stands before the company.
Lucy calls to Arthur to come to her, but Van Helsing holds up a crucifix and she recoils.
Arthur gives Van Helsing leave to proceed, and Van Helsing reseals the tomb after Lucy re-enters.
The men return to the tomb at night in black, with Van Helsing bringing a stake, hammer and tools.
Arthur agrees to drive the stake through Lucy's heart, and the others pray for her.
Arthur drives the stake through Lucy's heart, and her body writhes and then falls still.
The body inside the coffin now looks like Lucy in life, and Arthur is released from his torment.
The men promise to help Van Helsing find and stop the author of their sorrow.
Van Helsing arranges a dinner in two nights and leaves for Amsterdam, promising to return and explain the great quest.
Mina Harker telegraphs Dr. Seward that she is coming to London and that Jonathan is at Whitby with important news.
Van Helsing gives Seward the typed diaries of Jonathan and Mina and leaves for Liverpool Street, asking him to study them before they meet again.
Mina goes to Seward's study and learns he keeps his diary on a phonograph, which he refuses to let her hear about Lucy's death.
Mina persuades Seward that she can be trusted by pointing to her own and Jonathan's diaries, and he agrees to let her hear the cylinders.
Seward agrees to let Mina help with the records, and she begins typewriting the cylinders for the group's shared knowledge.
Mina hears the story of Lucy's death on the phonograph and is overwhelmed, comforted only that Lucy is at peace.
Jonathan Harker arrives at Seward's house, and he and Mina begin collating every scrap of evidence in chronological order.
Seward realises the house next door to the asylum may be the Count's hiding place, a clue the group had overlooked.
Seward finds Renfield unusually calm and suspects his contentment is tied to the Count's ultimate triumph; he orders close watch.
Harker travels to Whitby, where Billington gives him the papers showing the consignment of fifty cases of earth.
Harker confirms at King's Cross that the boxes received there match the original invoice.
Harker traces the boxes to Carter Paterson and confirms they were delivered to Carfax, establishing they are in the old chapel.
Lord Godalming and Quincey Morris arrive early; Mina gives them copies of the typed records and tells them she knows of their proposals to Lucy.
Arthur breaks down in grief, and Mina comforts him like a sister and promises to help him if he needs it.
Mina comforts Morris and promises to be his friend, and he kisses her hand and calls her a little girl, as he once called Lucy.
Mrs. Harker visits Renfield, who unsettles her with his remarks, and she leaves with Seward.
Renfield confesses that he once tried to kill Seward to absorb his life through the blood, then bids Mrs. Harker farewell with a curse-like blessing.
Seward learns that Dracula's house is next to his own, and Van Helsing regrets not knowing sooner.
All records are completed and ordered for the group's meeting.
The men and Mina join hands with Van Helsing in a solemn compact to destroy the vampire.
Van Helsing lays out the vampire's limitations and powers, and his suspected identity as Voivode Dracula.
The group plans to trace the remaining boxes of earth, which are the vampire's refuge.
A shot shatters the window; Quincey Morris explains he fired at a bat.
The men decide Mina must be kept out of the danger and told nothing more.
The men go to Carfax with the means to enter Dracula's house, leaving Mina behind.
Renfield urgently requests to see Seward, and the group goes to his room.
Renfield begs to be released that very night, refusing to reveal his true reasons.
Renfield breaks down, pleads and weeps, but Seward refuses and calms him, and he sits down quietly.
The men go to the Count's house in the moonlight, keeping to the shadows, and enter it with skeleton keys.
In the small chapel the party finds the earth-boxes and counts twenty-nine of the original fifty remaining.
Rats swarm the chapel and Lord Godalming summons his terriers, who drive the rats away.
Van Helsing judges the night successful, noting the Count's power over rats is limited and that the Count is elsewhere.
Jonathan resolves to keep Mina ignorant of the night's work and to protect her from further horror.
Twenty-one boxes are now known to have been removed, and Jonathan plans to trace them through Thomas Snelling.
Seward recalls Renfield's claim of consuming living things, which he made while his mouth was still nauseous from flies and spiders.
Van Helsing visits Renfield, who insults him and refuses to talk, so Van Helsing gives up learning from him.
Van Helsing goes to confer with Mina and Jonathan, while Quincey and Arthur follow clues about the earth-boxes.
Mina has a frightening dream of a red-eyed fog pouring into her room and a pale face bending over her.
Renfield asks to see Mina, kisses her hand and blesses her, and Mina takes a sleeping draught from Seward.
Jonathan learns from the carrier Smollet where the first boxes were delivered, and that boxes went to Chicksand Street and Jamaica Lane.
Smollet says a carrier named Sam Bloxam may know more about another dusty job at a house, and promises to send the address.
Bloxam tells Jonathan he moved nine boxes from Purfleet to a house in Piccadilly, where the old man met him and helped carry them in.
Jonathan finds the Piccadilly house, which seems long empty, and learns from the mews that it was recently taken and sold through Mitchell, Sons & Candy.
Jonathan obtains the house agents' help by claiming to act for Lord Godalming, who once rented chambers through them.
The men agree that if all the boxes are found in the Piccadilly house the end is near, but they have no way yet to get inside.
Seward questions Renfield, who speaks of commanding destiny and wanting life rather than souls, and hints at a friend who will keep him supplied.
Seward and Van Helsing find Renfield calmly singing and folding a scrap of paper, and learn nothing from him.
The agents reply to Lord Godalming that the Piccadilly house was bought by a foreign nobleman, Count de Ville, paying in notes.
Seward posts a man in the corridor to listen to Renfield, who is seen sleeping soundly that evening.
The men plan to keep horses ready and sterilise the imported earth between sunrise and sunset to catch the Count at his weakest.
A yell comes from Renfield's room and he is found on the floor, covered in blood after some accident.
Seward finds Renfield on the floor in a pool of blood with terrible injuries to his face, back and limbs.
Van Helsing comes to the room and, understanding the danger, asks that the attendant be sent away before Renfield wakes.
Van Helsing decides to trephine Renfield's skull to relieve the pressure from his brain injury.
After the operation Renfield wakes briefly and begins to tell his story of the Count entering his room.
Renfield describes fighting the Count to protect Mrs. Harker, then the mist escaping under the door.
The men arm themselves and rush to the Harkers' room, sensing the Count is there.
The men break open the Harkers' door and find the Count feeding on Mina, who is held down while Jonathan lies in a stupor.
The Count flees under the door as the men hold up crucifixes and the Sacred Wafer, leaving a faint vapour behind.
Van Helsing wakes Jonathan with cold water while Mina sobs, and Quincey is seen hiding under a yew tree.
Arthur reports that the Count burned the manuscript and the phonograph cylinders and that Renfield is dead.
Quincey reports seeing a bat fly westward from Renfield's window, and believes the Count has gone to another lair.
Mina begins to recount her ordeal, describing how the Count drank her blood and forced her to drink from his breast.
Renfield is found dead on the floor of his room, and Seward plans to certify death by misadventure, keeping the truth from the coroner.
The group decides Mina must be told everything, and she says she would kill herself if she found she harmed someone she loves.
Van Helsing forbids Mina from dying by any hand, including her own, until the Count is truly destroyed, and she promises to try to live.
Van Helsing argues the Count's lairs can be sterilised and that the Piccadilly house may hold the key, so the group plans to search it.
Van Helsing proposes entering the Piccadilly house by hiring a locksmith openly, so the police will not interfere.
Mina insists that Jonathan and the others go on the expedition, saying the group's combined strength is her last hope.
The Sacred Wafer burns into Mina's forehead when Van Helsing places it there, and she collapses in grief, believing she is unclean.
Van Helsing tells Mina the scar may remain until the Judgment Day, offering hope that it will one day pass away.
The men kneel and swear to be true to each other and to raise the veil of sorrow from Mina.
At Carfax the group finds the house unchanged and opens the great earth-boxes, placing a portion of the Host in each to sterilise them.
Godalming and Morris go to find a locksmith, leaving the others to wait in the Green Park.
A locksmith opens the Piccadilly house, and Godalming and Morris let the others in.
In the dining-room the group finds eight of the nine earth-boxes, along with title deeds and a ring of keys, and Godalming and Morris take the keys to destroy the remaining lairs.
A telegram from Mina warns that the Count has left Carfax heading south and may want to see them.
Godalming and Morris return, reporting they destroyed the earth-boxes at both places.
The Count bursts into the room, is struck at by Harker, and escapes through the window, leaving money behind.
The Count boasts that his revenge will spread over centuries and that the girls they love are already his.
The group returns to Seward's house, where Mina greets them and Jonathan is left broken, with one earth-box still unfound.
Morris is found keeping watch outside the room, and Mina is comforted that brave men guard her.
Mina asks for Van Helsing to hypnotise her before dawn so she can speak, and he does.
Under hypnosis Mina reveals she is on a ship, hearing water and a capstan, and the men realise the Count is fleeing London by sea.
Van Helsing tells Mina they must follow the Count even into hell because he can live for centuries and her throat bears his mark.
Mina faints as Van Helsing speaks of the danger she faces, and Seward catches her.
Left London by ship for Varna, having had a box of earth carried aboard the Czarina Catherine.
Van Helsing and the others trace the Count's escape to the Czarina Catherine, a Black Sea-bound ship leaving on the tide.
Dock men report that a thin, pale stranger hurried aboard with a large box and then vanished into fog as the ship left.
The party learns the box is to be landed at Varna and handed to an agent named Ristics, and resolves to act themselves.
Mina says Jonathan must not go on the pursuit and asks to be taken along; Van Helsing reasons that the Count is a danger to them all.
Van Helsing insists the Count must be destroyed for the sake of Mina and humanity, warning that he is a threat that grows.
The group agrees to sleep on their conclusions and meet at breakfast to fix a course of action.
Morris proposes adding Winchester rifles to the party's arms, and the plan is set to leave for Varna by the 17th.
Van Helsing assumes only four will travel, leaving Harker behind to guard his wife, and Harker asks to discuss it with Mina.
Mina asks Jonathan to promise on his honour that he will tell her nothing of the plans, and he gives his word, shutting a door between them.
Mina tells Van Helsing that she must go on the journey, because the Count can command her and she may betray the plans without knowing it.
Van Helsing tells Godalming, Seward and Morris that Mina will come, and the men plan to board the ship at Varna with wild rose and firearms.
Harker settles his affairs and makes his will, leaving Mina his sole heir, ready for whatever the pursuit brings.
Jonathan and the party reach Varna by train and wait for the Czarina Catherine, with Mina's trance reports indicating the ship is still at sea.
The party plans to board the ship between sunrise and sunset, when the Count cannot leave his box, and open it to destroy him.
Godalming secures permission from the shippers to open the box, and the Vice-Consul's agent is won over to aid them.
Mina falls into a deep lethargy, and Van Helsing and Seward grow troubled, fearing the change in her and its dreaded remedy.
Van Helsing fears the Count is escaping them and suspects Mina's trance may have carried her memories in unexpected ways.
A telegram reports the Czarina Catherine has entered Galatz, so the Count has escaped the party's trap.
Mina reveals she knows the train times and that the only train to Galatz leaves at 6:30 the next morning.
Van Helsing assigns tasks: Godalming to the train, Harker to the shipping agent, Morris to the Vice-Consul, and Seward to stay with Mina.
Mina offers a clear reading of the Count as a selfish criminal who flees danger, which Van Helsing takes as proof her mind is freer.
Mina feels her soul freed somewhat from the Count's power, though fears he may have used her knowledge in trance.
Van Helsing declares the Count has cut himself off from knowing the group's whereabouts, and that Mina's connection gives them an advantage.
Under hypnosis Mina reports the ship is still, with men's voices, oars and a gleam of light.
Van Helsing reasons the Count must reach land by night, since daylight would expose him in his box.
At dawn Mina reports only darkness, lapping water and creaking wood, and the party must wait for night.
Mina's trance at sunrise reveals cattle lowing and a strange sound, but she wakes unable to remember.
Mina goes to the hotel at Galatz while Lord Godalming visits the Vice-Consul and the others go to the shipping agents.
Captain Donelson describes the box put aboard at London and the crew's fear of it, before handing it off at Galatz.
Hildesheim reveals he gave the box to Skinsky, who was paid in English banknote and took it away.
Skinsky is found dead in St. Peter's churchyard with his throat torn open, ending the trail.
Mina is released from her promise and taken fully into the party's confidence.
Mina types the party's records and studies the papers while the men rest.
Mina deduces the Count arranged water transport through Skinsky and then killed his agent.
Mina concludes the box travelled on a river, probably the Sereth or Pruth, by oars or poles.
Lord Godalming plans to follow the box by steam launch on the river.
Mr. Morris plans to take horses along the bank in case the box is landed.
Dr. Seward resolves to ride with Quincey Morris, and Jonathan is torn between Mina and the boat.
Van Helsing decides to take Mina overland toward the Count's castle through the Borgo Pass.
Van Helsing argues he must take Mina to save her from the Count's castle, and Jonathan reluctantly consents.
Mina and Van Helsing prepare to leave by train for Veresti, and Mina says a painful farewell to Jonathan.
Lord Godalming and Jonathan steam up the river, reasoning the Sereth and Bistritza are the likely route.
At Fundu the party gets a Roumanian flag and boats treat them deferentially, though none has seen the box.
Dr. Seward and Quincey Morris ride for three days without news and push on.
The launch is delayed at the rapids and then resumes the chase, though it may be damaged.
Mina and Van Helsing reach Veresti at noon, and Van Helsing buys a carriage and horses for the seventy-mile drive.
Van Helsing and Mina reach the Borgo Pass at sunrise, and Mina leads them down a little-used by-road.
Mina wakes unusually bright and cannot be hypnotised again, and Van Helsing grows afraid of her unnatural health.
At night three female figures materialise from mist and snow outside the holy circle and call Mina to join them.
At dawn the figures vanish, and the horses are found dead; Mina sleeps deeply and cannot be woken.
Van Helsing goes alone to the castle, destroys three Un-Dead women in their tombs and banishes the Count's tomb with the Wafer.
Mina wakes and urges Van Helsing away from the castle to meet Jonathan, whom she knows is coming.
From a rock shelter Mina and Van Helsing see the gypsy cart and the approaching riders as the sun nears the mountains.
Jonathan, Godalming, Seward and Morris halt the gypsies, and Jonathan and Morris break open the great box.
Jonathan cuts through the Count's throat and Morris drives a knife into his heart, and the body crumbles to dust at sunset.
The survivors travel to Transylvania and find the castle standing above a desolate waste, with every trace of the past erased.
At home, they review the papers and find almost no authentic documents, only typewriting and private note-books, so no one could readily be asked to accept the story as proof.
Van Helsing declares that no proofs are wanted, and says the boy will one day understand how brave his mother is and how men loved her enough to dare much for her.

recaps.text: Harker travels east through Hungary and Transylvania, writing a journal, and learns about the region's superstitions. At Bistritz, the landlady and others react with fear to Harker's destination, Count Dracula's castle. Count Dracula's letter instructs Harker to take the coach to the Borgo Pass, where a carriage will meet him. Harker is given a crucifix by the landlady and wears it despite his unease. On the coach, passengers cross themselves and offer Harker charms against the evil eye. No carriage awaits at the Pass, but a black calèche arrives driven by a tall, pale-eyed stranger. The driver takes Harker's luggage and sends the coach onward to Bukovina. During the night journey, dogs and wolves howl, and blue flames appear on the road. Wolves surround the carriage, and the driver drives them off with a gesture. The carriage arrives at a vast ruined castle with dark, unlit windows.
recaps.title: CHAPTER I JONATHAN HARKER’S JOURNAL

recaps.text: Jonathan Harker, an English solicitor, travels to Transylvania to help Count Dracula buy an estate near London, after Peter Hawkins arranged the trip. Along the way he meets fearful locals, a stranger driver with unnatural strength, and wolves that flee the carriage. He reaches the Count's vast ruined castle, where the Count welcomes him courteously but avoids food and mirrors. The two discuss English life and the purchase of Carfax at Purfleet, while the Count shows strange habits and a repugnant touch. Harker's crucifix stops the Count's rage after he cuts himself shaving, and the Count smashes the glass. Harker finds the castle's doors locked and realises he is a prisoner. He remains there, uneasy, with only the Count for company.

Harker arrives at Castle Dracula late at night and is welcomed by the Count, who carries his luggage and serves him supper. The Count asks many questions about England and studies English books and maps. The Count reviews the purchase of the Carfax estate at Purfleet with Harker and shows interest in its location. Harker notices the Count casts no reflection in the shaving glass and is troubled by his strange presence. Harker cuts himself while shaving, and the Count's fury at the blood subsides when he touches the crucifix. The Count smashes the shaving glass and leaves, and Harker is left alone for the day. Harker explores the castle, finds every door locked, and concludes that he is a prisoner.
recaps.title: CHAPTER II JONATHAN HARKER’S JOURNAL—continued

recaps.text: Jonathan Harker, an English solicitor, travelled to Transylvania at the request of Peter Hawkins to help Count Dracula buy property near London. Along the way he met fearful locals and unnatural threats, then reached the Count's ruined castle, where he learned he was a prisoner. The Count controls the household and reads Harker's letters, and Harker has resolved to hide his fears and watch carefully. Harker has found that the Count climbs the castle walls and that no servants exist, leading him to suspect the Count is more than human. Harker found a forgotten wing, slept in an old ladies' room, and was attacked by three women who could not cast shadows. The Count violently intervened, claimed Harker as his own, and sent the women away, after which Harker fainted. Harker now remains a prisoner, uncertain of his fate and in fear for his sanity.

Harker concludes he cannot trust the Count and decides to hide his fears and watch carefully. Harker deduces that the Count may be the driver who brought him and that no servants exist in the castle. The Count talks proudly of his ancestors and the warlike history of the Szekely race. The Count quizzes Harker on English legal practice and insists he stay a month longer. Harker finds the Count has been reading his letters and resolves to write openly only to Hawkins and Mina. Harker secretly reads two unsealed letters before the Count returns and collects them. The Count warns Harker to stay only in his own rooms, which Harker resolves to obey. Harker watches the Count climb down the castle wall like a lizard and is terrified. Harker discovers a disused wing of the castle and finds the main door locked with its key missing. Harker falls asleep in the old ladies' room and is visited by three women who try to bite him. The Count violently intervenes, claims Harker for himself, and sends the women away with a struggling bag. Harker faints in horror, unsure whether the events were a dream.
recaps.title: CHAPTER III JONATHAN HARKER’S JOURNAL—continued

recaps.text: Jonathan Harker, an English solicitor, travelled to Transylvania to help Count Dracula buy property near London. At the castle he discovered he was a prisoner, the Count controls and reads his letters, and no servants exist. Harker was attacked by three women who cast no shadows, the Count drove them off, and Harker has since watched the Count climb the walls and seen him wear Harker's own clothes. The Count has sent letters postdated to later dates and is preparing for Harker's departure, while boxes of earth are being taken out of the castle. Harker found the Count lying in a box in a ruined chapel below the castle and struck at him with a shovel, but was stopped by the Count's gaze. Now Harker is locked in the Count's room as the Szgany and Slovaks leave with their boxes, and he plans to climb the wall and flee, leaving the castle alone with the women.

Harker finds his door fastened from outside and discovers the Count has taken his papers, money and clothes. Harker watches the Slovaks deliver heavy boxes and sees the Count leave by the window wearing Harker's clothes. Harker is drawn into a hypnotic trance by moonbeams and is terrified by the three women forming in the light. Harker climbs the castle wall to the Count's room and finds the gold hoard and a stairway down to a ruined chapel. In the chapel Harker finds the Count lying apparently dead in a box of earth, and is nearly overcome by hatred and horror. The Count announces Harker's departure but then opens the great door to the wolves, and Harker begs for it to be shut. Harker enters the Count's room again, finds the boxes nailed shut, and is locked in as the carts depart. Harker resolves to climb the castle wall and escape, believing death is preferable to remaining with the women.
recaps.title: CHAPTER IV JONATHAN HARKER’S JOURNAL—continued

recaps.text: Jonathan Harker, an English solicitor, travelled to Transylvania to help Count Dracula buy property near London. At the castle he found he was a prisoner, that the Count controls his letters, and that no servants exist. Three women who cast no shadows attacked him, and the Count drove them off. Harker has watched the Count climb walls and wear Harker's clothes, and the Count has been preparing to send Harker away while boxes of earth leave the castle. Harker found the Count lying in a box in a ruined chapel and struck at him, but was stopped by the Count's gaze. Harker was then locked in the Count's room as the carts departed and resolved to escape by climbing the castle wall. Meanwhile in London, Mina Murray writes to Lucy Westenra about her engagement to Jonathan, who is still abroad. Lucy confesses her love for Arthur Holmwood and then turns down two proposals, from Dr. John Seward and Quincey P. Morris, and accepts a third. Dr. Seward, rebuffed, questions his patient Renfield, and Quincey invites Arthur and Seward to a gathering. Harker's fate at the castle remains unresolved.

Mina Murray writes to Lucy Westenra about her work, her shorthand practice, and her engagement to Jonathan Harker, who is abroad. Lucy confides to Mina that she loves Arthur Holmwood, though he has not yet told her so. Lucy receives three marriage proposals in one day, from Dr. John Seward, Quincey P. Morris and a third man, and she refuses the first two. Dr. Seward, rebuffed, throws himself into work and questions his patient Renfield closely about his delusions. Quincey P. Morris invites Arthur Holmwood and Dr. Seward to a gathering, and Arthur accepts with a message.
recaps.title: CHAPTER V

recaps.text: Jonathan Harker, an English solicitor, went to Transylvania to help Count Dracula buy property near London and found himself a prisoner at the castle, where the Count controls his letters and has sent carts of earth away. Harker struck at the Count in a ruined chapel and was stopped by his gaze, then was locked in and resolved to escape over the castle wall. In London, Mina Murray writes to Lucy Westenra about her engagement to Jonathan, who is still abroad. Lucy confesses her love for Arthur Holmwood and refuses two proposals, from Dr. John Seward and Quincey P. Morris, while accepting a third. Seward, rebuffed, studies his patient Renfield, who collects and devours living creatures. Mina has now gone to Whitby with Lucy, where old Mr. Swales talks of tombstones and the dead. Mina has had only a short letter from Jonathan, dated from the castle and saying he is starting for home, and Lucy has resumed sleepwalking. Arthur is delayed by his father's illness, and a storm is coming. Jonathan's fate and whereabouts remain unresolved.

Mina travels to Whitby, where Lucy shows her the harbour and churchyard above the town. Old Mr. Swales mocks the local legends and tombstones, while Mina and Lucy read the inscriptions with him. Lucy tells Mina of her coming marriage to Arthur, and Mina admits she has heard nothing from Jonathan for a month. Dr. Seward watches Renfield closely and discovers that he is devouring the living creatures he collects, which Seward names a life-devouring mania. Mina receives a brief letter from Jonathan from Castle Dracula, saying he is starting for home, which leaves her uneasy. Lucy's sleepwalking resumes, and Mina agrees to lock their door at night. Arthur is delayed in Ring because his father is ill, and Lucy frets at the wait. Mina hears no news from Jonathan, while a storm approaches and a Russian ship behaves oddly off the coast. Mr. Swales confides to Mina that he expects to die soon and apologises for his earlier mockery.
recaps.title: CHAPTER VI MINA MURRAY’S JOURNAL

recaps.text: A Russian schooner, the Demeter, runs into Whitby harbour in a storm with a dead steersman lashed to her wheel. The coastguard and a doctor examine the body, which had been dead about two days, and the steersman is removed to the mortuary. The ship's cargo of boxes of earth is taken possession of by a Whitby solicitor, and an immense dog is seen fleeing from the ship. The captain's log and a paper from a bottle reveal that the crew vanished one by one and the mate went mad. The mate throws himself into the sea, and the captain vows to bind himself to the wheel rather than abandon the ship. The town plans a public funeral for the captain, and the dog remains untraced. Mina finds Lucy sleepwalking again and worries deeply about Jonathan, who has not been heard from. At the captain's funeral a dog cowers in terror, and Mr. Swales is found dead on the bench with a look of horror. Mina resolves to take Lucy on a long walk to tire her out before sleep.
recaps.title: CHAPTER VII CUTTING FROM “THE DAILYGRAPH,” 8 AUGUST

recaps.text: Jonathan Harker, an English solicitor, went to Transylvania on business for Peter Hawkins and became a prisoner in Castle Dracula, where Count Dracula controlled his letters and sent crates of earth away. Harker escaped and fell gravely ill. In London, Mina Murray's dearest friend Lucy Westenra accepted Arthur Holmwood's proposal after refusing others, and Dr. John Seward studies his patient Renfield, who devours living creatures. At Whitby, Lucy sleepwalked, the Demeter arrived with a dead steersman and vanished crew, and Mr. Swales was found dead. Mina has now learned that Jonathan has been ill in a Buda-Pesth hospital for six weeks and resolves to go to him. Lucy's health continues to fail, and her mother is secretly dying. Fifty boxes have been delivered to Carfax. Renfield has escaped, been caught, and is chained in a padded room, raving of his master. Jonathan's full recovery, Lucy's condition, and the nature of the Master remain unresolved.

Mina finds Lucy, who has been fading, at last improving, and Lucy recalls a dreamlike sense of being drawn towards the sea. Lucy's mother privately tells Mina that her heart is failing and that she may die within months, and asks Mina to keep it hidden. Samuel F. Billington & Son arrange for Carter, Paterson & Co. to carry fifty boxes to Carfax, and the goods are delivered there. Mina receives news that Jonathan Harker has been seriously ill, and resolves to travel to Buda-Pesth to nurse him and bring him home. A nursing sister writes that Jonathan has been ill for six weeks and has spoken of his engagement to Mina. Renfield becomes haughty and declares the Master is at hand, and Dr. Seward observes him closely. Renfield escapes through a window, and Seward pursues him to the walls of Carfax, where he is heard pleading to a master. Renfield is overpowered after a violent struggle and chained in a padded room, raving of his master and of waiting for the Master.
recaps.title: CHAPTER VIII MINA MURRAY’S JOURNAL

recaps.text: Jonathan Harker, an English solicitor, was imprisoned in Count Dracula's castle in Transylvania, escaped, and fell gravely ill, while Count Dracula sent fifty boxes of earth to Carfax. In London, Lucy Westenra, Mina's dearest friend, accepted Arthur Holmwood's proposal, and at Whitby she sleepwalked, and the Demeter arrived with a dead crew. Mina travelled to Buda-Pesth and married the recovering Jonathan, who gave her his secret notebook to keep sealed. Lucy's health has collapsed, her mother is privately dying of a heart condition, and Arthur has asked Dr. Seward to examine her. Dr. Seward finds no physical cause and has summoned Van Helsing, who examined Lucy and promised to return if needed. Renfield, held in a padded room at Dr. Seward's asylum, shifts between violence and calm with the time of day and keeps escaping toward Carfax. Lucy's condition suddenly worsened on 6 September, and Dr. Seward has urged Van Helsing to hurry to London. The cause of Lucy's illness and the nature of the Master remain unresolved.

Mina writes from Buda-Pesth that she has married Jonathan Harker, who is weak and has lost his memory of recent events. Jonathan gives Mina his private notebook and asks her never to read it unless duty demands, and she seals it under her wedding ring. Lucy writes from Whitby that she is well, engaged to Arthur Holmwood, and due to marry on 28 September. Renfield's violent fits recur, and he begins to calm under the moon, asking to be given sugar and flies. Renfield escapes again toward the old chapel at Carfax, and afterwards goes back quietly, which troubles Dr. Seward. Lucy grows weaker and her mother secretly reveals her own heart disease, so Arthur asks Dr. Seward to examine Lucy. Dr. Seward finds Lucy's blood normal and suspects a mental cause, so he summons Van Helsing from Amsterdam. Van Helsing examines Lucy, finds no bodily cause, and leaves to think, promising to return if needed. Renfield's moods again follow the time of day, with a violent fit at noon and a calm after sunset. On 6 September Dr. Seward telegraphs Van Helsing that Lucy has suddenly become much worse and urges him to come at once.
recaps.title: CHAPTER IX

recaps.text: Jonathan Harker, an English solicitor, was imprisoned in Count Dracula's castle in Transylvania, escaped, and fell ill, while Dracula sent fifty boxes of earth to Carfax. In London, Lucy Westenra accepted Arthur Holmwood's proposal and has been sleepwalking and growing weak, and Mina married Jonathan in Buda-Pesth. Dr. Seward, who runs an asylum and watches the patient Renfield, could find no physical cause for Lucy's decline and summoned Van Helsing from Amsterdam. Lucy's condition collapsed on 6 September. Van Helsing arrived, judged her near death from blood loss, and gave a transfusion using Arthur's blood, then noticed two small punctures on her throat that neither doctor can explain. Van Helsing left for Amsterdam and ordered Dr. Seward to keep watch, but Lucy was found almost dead again the next morning and given a second transfusion. The doctors have sworn to keep the transfusions secret from Arthur, and Van Helsing has surrounded Lucy with garlic. The cause of Lucy's illness, the marks on her throat, and the nature of the Master remain unresolved.

Dr. Seward meets Van Helsing in London and they agree to keep Lucy's true condition hidden from Arthur and from Mrs. Westenra. Van Helsing urges Dr. Seward to record every doubt and detail, and examines Lucy, finding her near death from blood loss. Arthur arrives unexpectedly and offers his blood, and Van Helsing performs a transfusion using Arthur's blood. Van Helsing notices two small punctures on Lucy's throat, which Dr. Seward cannot explain, and Van Helsing leaves for Amsterdam, ordering Dr. Seward to keep watch. Dr. Seward sits up with Lucy through a peaceful night, then goes home exhausted and is told by Van Helsing that he will return. On the next morning Dr. Seward finds Lucy almost dead again, and he and Van Helsing give her a second transfusion and a morphia injection. Van Helsing swears Dr. Seward to silence about the transfusions so Arthur is not frightened or jealous. Van Helsing surrounds Lucy with garlic flowers and seals her room, and Dr. Seward is left uneasy by his confidence.
recaps.title: CHAPTER X

recaps.text: Jonathan Harker escaped from Count Dracula's castle in Transylvania and fell ill, while Dracula sent fifty boxes of earth to Carfax. In London, Lucy Westenra, engaged to Arthur Holmwood, has been sleepwalking and growing weak, and Mina married Jonathan in Buda-Pesth. Dr. Seward could find no physical cause for Lucy's decline and summoned Van Helsing, who gave her blood transfusions and noticed two punctures on her throat. The doctors keep the transfusions secret from Arthur, and Van Helsing surrounds Lucy with garlic. Lucy has recovered for a few days, and Van Helsing went to Amsterdam, but Mrs. Westenra removed the flowers and opened the window. Dr. Seward attacked by a patient, Renfield, and an escaped wolf has been seen in London. That night, the wolf broke into Lucy's room, Mrs. Westenra died, and Lucy found the maids drugged with laudanum. Lucy is alone with her mother's body, has written a farewell, and fears she may not survive the night, while Van Helsing's telegram is delayed and Dr. Seward is not yet at Hillingham.

Van Helsing is distressed to learn that Mrs. Westenra removed the garlic flowers from Lucy's room, and he resolves to act immediately. Dr. Seward gives Lucy another transfusion, and Van Helsing takes over her care for the next two nights, insisting the flowers must stay. Lucy recovers over four days, her nightmares fading, and Van Helsing departs for Amsterdam. At the Zoological Gardens, the keeper Thomas Bilder describes how the wolf Bersicker escaped after a provocative stranger upset the animals. Bersicker returns on his own, and the keeper locks him back in his cage. Dr. Seward is attacked by a patient with a dinner-knife, and the patient is subdued while licking up the blood from his wound. Van Helsing telegraphs urgent instructions for Dr. Seward to be at Hillingham that night, but the message arrives late. That night the wolf breaks into Lucy's room and Mrs. Westenra dies of fright. Lucy finds the servants drugged and her mother's laudanum gone, leaving her alone with the body. Lucy writes a memorandum and bids farewell to Arthur, fearing she may not survive the night.
recaps.title: CHAPTER XI

recaps.text: Jonathan Harker escaped Count Dracula's castle and fell ill, while Dracula shipped boxes of earth to Carfax. In London Lucy Westenra, engaged to Arthur Holmwood, sleepwalked and weakened, and Van Helsing and Dr. Seward gave her blood transfusions and noticed puncture wounds on her throat. Renfield, an asylum patient, attacked Seward, and a wolf broke into Lucy's room the night her mother died of fright. Seward and Van Helsing forced entry into Hillingham, revived Lucy with brandy, warm baths and a transfusion from Quincey Morris, then Lucy wakened, received Arthur, and died at dawn. Van Helsing warns that her death is only the beginning, and Seward and Quincey stand ready to help what follows.

Dr. Seward reaches Hillingham and, with Van Helsing, breaks in through a kitchen window to find the servants drugged and Lucy near death beside her dead mother. The doctors revive Lucy with brandy, warm baths and another transfusion, this time using Quincey Morris's blood after he arrives with a message from Arthur. Lucy wakes weakly, weeps for her mother, and in her sleep tears up a paper Van Helsing had found on her breast. Seward plans to certify Mrs. Westenra's death as heart failure to avoid an inquest, and admits to Quincey that Lucy has been receiving transfusions for ten days. Arthur arrives later and Lucy rallies briefly in his presence, but she grows worse through the night. At dawn Van Helsing finds Lucy's throat wounds gone and declares her dying, and she calls Arthur to kiss her in a changed, voluptuous voice. Van Helsing pulls Arthur away and then swears to Lucy to guard him, and Lucy dies, though Van Helsing warns that her death is only the beginning.
recaps.title: CHAPTER XII DR. SEWARD’S DIARY

recaps.text: Jonathan Harker escaped Count Dracula's castle and fell ill, while Dracula shipped boxes of earth to Carfax. In London Lucy Westenra, engaged to Arthur Holmwood, sleepwalked and weakened, and Van Helsing and Dr. Seward gave her blood transfusions and noticed throat wounds. Lucy died at dawn after a final attempt to save her, and her mother died of fright earlier. Van Helsing took Lucy's papers, proposed a secret post-mortem, then abandoned it after a stolen crucifix was recovered. Mrs. Westenra's estate passed wholly to Arthur, who accepted Van Helsing's keeping of Lucy's papers. Mina and Jonathan, now married, attended a funeral in London and Jonathan saw the Count in Piccadilly. Lucy and Mrs. Westenra are buried, Arthur has returned to Ring, and Van Helsing has left for Amsterdam, promising to return to Seward. Children on Hampstead Heath are being lured away by a bloofer lady and found with throat wounds, and the matter is now public. Unresolved are Van Helsing's secret knowledge, the stolen crucifix, the Count's presence in England, and the Hampstead attacks.

Van Helsing searches Lucy's papers and takes away letters and a diary he intends to keep from strangers. Van Helsing plans a secret post-mortem, cutting off Lucy's head and taking her heart, and asks Seward to help him do it at night. Seward protests but agrees, trusting Van Helsing, although Van Helsing later reveals that the gold crucifix was stolen and recovered, leaving the post-mortem abandoned. The solicitor Mr. Marquand explains that Mrs. Westenra left her whole estate to Arthur Holmwood. Arthur grieves at Lucy's bedside and accepts Van Helsing's request to hold her papers for a time. Mina and Jonathan attend Mr. Hawkins's funeral, and Jonathan is shaken by a glimpse of a dark, thin man he believes is the Count. Mina learns of the deaths of Mrs. Westenra and Lucy by telegram from Van Helsing. Seward reflects on the burial and Van Helsing's strange laughter, and Van Helsing departs for Amsterdam. A Westminster Gazette report describes children on Hampstead Heath being lured away by a bloofer lady, and another child is found wounded in the throat.
recaps.title: CHAPTER XIII DR. SEWARD’S DIARY—continued.

recaps.text: Jonathan Harker escaped Count Dracula's castle and fell ill, while the Count shipped boxes of earth to London. In London, Lucy Westenra, engaged to Arthur Holmwood, sleepwalked and weakened, and Van Helsing and Dr. Seward gave her blood transfusions and noticed throat wounds. Lucy died, and her mother died of fright earlier; Arthur inherited the estate. Mina and Jonathan, now married, attended a funeral where Jonathan believed he saw the Count in London. Children on Hampstead Heath have been found with throat wounds. Mina has now given Van Helsing typed copies of Jonathan's journal, and Van Helsing has confirmed that the journal is true and that Jonathan is sound of mind. Van Helsing has also reported children with throat wounds at Hampstead and has told Seward that Lucy herself made those wounds. Unresolved are Van Helsing's secret knowledge, the stolen crucifix, the Count's presence in England, and what Van Helsing will do next.

Van Helsing visits Mina in Exeter and reads the typed account of Lucy's sleepwalking. Mina gives Van Helsing a typed copy of Jonathan's journal, which overwhelms her with fear and dread. Van Helsing confirms that Jonathan's journal is true and that Jonathan's mind is sound. Jonathan, reassured, meets Van Helsing and agrees to tell him what happened before Transylvania. Van Helsing reads a newspaper report of children with throat wounds at Hampstead and grows pale. Van Helsing tells Seward that the children's wounds were made by Lucy, a shocking claim Seward struggles to accept.
recaps.title: CHAPTER XIV MINA HARKER’S JOURNAL

recaps.text: Jonathan Harker escaped Count Dracula's castle and fell ill, while the Count shipped boxes of earth to London. In London, Lucy Westenra sleepwalked and weakened, and Van Helsing and Dr. Seward gave her blood transfusions and noticed throat wounds. Lucy died, and her mother died earlier; Arthur inherited the estate. Children on Hampstead Heath have been found with throat wounds. Van Helsing has told Seward that Lucy made those wounds, and Seward has resisted the claim. Van Helsing confessed that Lucy is Un-Dead and took Seward to the hospital child, then to Lucy's tomb. The coffin was found empty, then Lucy was found lifelike in the tomb with sharp teeth. Van Helsing plans to destroy her body, and Arthur has agreed to join him at the churchyard. Unresolved are Lucy's fate, the Count's presence in England, and what Van Helsing will do next.

Van Helsing confesses to Seward that Lucy is Un-Dead and says the bitten child proves it. Seward is angry, but Van Helsing asks him to accompany him to the child and then the tomb. At the hospital, Dr. Vincent shows the child's punctures, which resemble Lucy's, and attributes them to an animal. At the churchyard, Van Helsing opens Lucy's coffin and finds it empty, leaving Seward unconvinced. Van Helsing then finds a child in the churchyard and carries it out, and the two take it to the Heath. On the next day, Van Helsing reopens the tomb and finds Lucy lifelike and fresh, with sharp teeth. Van Helsing says Lucy must be destroyed, and Seward begins to accept his theories despite himself. Van Helsing decides to wait, leaves a note about watching the tomb, and plans to bring Arthur and Quincey in. Arthur refuses to allow any mutilation of Lucy's body and protests angrily to Van Helsing. Van Helsing pleads with Arthur, and Arthur reluctantly agrees to go to the churchyard and wait.
recaps.title: CHAPTER XV DR. SEWARD’S DIARY—continued.

recaps.text: Jonathan Harker escaped Count Dracula's castle and fell ill, while the Count shipped boxes of earth to London. In London Lucy Westenra sleepwalked and weakened, received blood transfusions, and died; her mother died earlier, and Arthur Holmwood inherited the estate. Children on Hampstead Heath were found with throat wounds, which Van Helsing blamed on Lucy, Un-Dead. Van Helsing took Seward to the child and then to Lucy's tomb, where the coffin was empty and then Lucy appeared lifelike. Arthur agreed to drive a stake through her heart, which laid her to rest in peace. The men now promise to find the author of their sorrow, and Van Helsing plans to return from Amsterdam for a dinner in two nights to reveal the quest.

The coffin is found empty and Lucy later appears alive in the churchyard, carrying a child and showing hellish eyes and blood on her lips. Van Helsing seals the tomb with consecrated bread and garlic, and Lucy's attempt to draw Arthur to her is stopped by a crucifix. On the next night the men return, and Arthur agrees to drive a stake through Lucy's heart while the others pray. After the stake is driven, Lucy's body appears peaceful, and Arthur is released from his torment. The men promise to find the author of their sorrow, and Van Helsing announces a dinner in two nights before leaving for Amsterdam.
recaps.title: CHAPTER XVI DR. SEWARD’S DIARY—continued

recaps.text: Mina Harker arrives at Dr. Seward's house and is given Van Helsing's papers to study before the group meets again. Seward is reluctant to let her hear his phonograph cylinders about Lucy's death, but he relents after she shows him her own and Jonathan's diaries. Mina learns the full story of Lucy's death and typewrites the cylinders, and the group begins collating their evidence in chronological order. Seward realises the house next door to the asylum may have been the Count's hiding place and watches Renfield's suspicious calm with growing alarm. Harker travels to Whitby and London and traces the fifty boxes of earth to the old chapel at Carfax. Lord Godalming and Quincey Morris arrive early, and Mina gives them the typed records and comforts Godalming in his grief. Mina promises to be a friend and helper to the men, and they accept her as one of the group.
recaps.title: CHAPTER XVII DR. SEWARD’S DIARY—continued

recaps.text: At a meeting, Van Helsing describes the vampire's great powers, the limits that restrict him, and the lore on how he may be destroyed. Van Helsing names Dracula as a former Voivode whose family is known for dealings with evil. Mina is kept out of danger, and the men plan to trace the boxes of earth and destroy the vampire. A shot from Quincey Morris breaks the window, which he claims was aimed at a bat. The men leave for Carfax to search Dracula's house, leaving Mina behind. Renfield then begs Seward and the others to release him that night, claiming important reasons he cannot explain. Seward refuses, and Renfield collapses into sullen calm, asking Seward to remember he tried to convince him.
recaps.title: CHAPTER XVIII DR. SEWARD’S DIARY

recaps.text: Jonathan Harker escaped Count Dracula's castle and fell ill, while the Count shipped fifty boxes of earth to London. In London Lucy Westenra sleepwalked, weakened, received transfusions, and died; her mother had died earlier. Children on Hampstead Heath were found with throat wounds, which Van Helsing blamed on Lucy, Un-Dead. Van Helsing and Seward staked Lucy's body, and Arthur agreed to drive the stake, laying her to rest. The men then resolved to find the Count and destroy him. They searched the Count's Carfax house and chapel, finding twenty-nine of fifty boxes still there, and learned that twenty-one boxes have been removed. Jonathan has kept the night's work secret from Mina, who is weak, unsettled by a dream, and kept out of further danger. Renfield, a patient who calls the Count his master, refuses to talk to Van Helsing. Things stand with the men still tracing the removed boxes while Mina rests.']}},

Van Helsing and the men enter the Count's house and chapel, finding twenty-nine of the fifty earth-boxes still there. Rats swarm the chapel until Lord Godalming's terriers drive them off, and the party leaves having learned the boxes' numbers. Twenty-one boxes are now known to have been removed, and Jonathan plans to trace the removals through Thomas Snelling. Van Helsing fails to learn anything from Renfield, who insults him and refuses to speak. Jonathan keeps the night's dangers from Mina, resolving she must be shielded from the work entirely. Mina, unsettled by a frightening dream and grief, feels weak and pleads for rest with Seward's sleeping draught.
recaps.title: CHAPTER XIX JONATHAN HARKER’S JOURNAL

recaps.text: Jonathan Harker escaped Count Dracula's castle and fell ill, while the Count shipped fifty boxes of earth to London. In London Lucy Westenra sleepwalked, weakened, and died after transfusions, and her mother had died earlier. Children on Hampstead Heath were found with throat wounds, which Van Helsing blamed on Lucy, Un-Dead; the men staked her body and resolved to find and destroy the Count. They searched the Carfax house and found twenty-nine of fifty boxes, learning that twenty-one have been removed. Jonathan has kept the night's work secret from Mina, who is weak and kept out of the danger. This stretch brings Jonathan's trace of the removed boxes: a carrier named Smollet gave a destination, then Bloxam described nine boxes moved to a house in Piccadilly, carried in by the old Count himself. The house is now sold to a Count de Ville. Renfield, who calls the Count his master, is silent and defiant toward Van Helsing and Seward, and at the end is found bloodied after a yell from his room. The men plan to break into the Piccadilly house and to sterilise the earth by day; the Count's whereabouts and the remaining boxes are unresolved.

Jonathan finds the carrier Thomas Snelling too drunk to help, so he goes to Walworth and speaks with Jack Smollet, who gives the destinations of the first boxes. Smollet names Sam Bloxam as a man who may know of another dusty job, and Jonathan pays for the address. Jonathan tracks Bloxam to a building site in Poplar and learns that nine boxes were moved to a house in Piccadilly by a strong old man with a white moustache. Bloxam reveals that the Count personally helped carry the boxes, showing the Count can handle the earth himself and is no longer confined to a single hiding place. Jonathan finds the Piccadilly house long empty and learns from the mews that it was recently taken and sold through Mitchell, Sons & Candy. The agents refuse to name the buyer until Jonathan claims to act for Lord Godalming, after which they promise to inform the lord by post. The men struggle to see how they can break into the Piccadilly house, and Lord Godalming plans to wait for the agency's reply. Seward tries to draw information from Renfield, who speaks of souls, life and a friend who will keep him supplied, and is evasive. The agents reply that the house was bought by a foreign nobleman, Count de Ville, paying in notes, which ties the purchase to the Count. The men decide to keep horses ready and sterilise the imported earth between sunrise and sunset to catch the Count at his weakest. Seward posts a watchman near Renfield, who is quiet overnight, then a wild yell is heard and Renfield is found bloodied on the floor.
recaps.title: CHAPTER XX JONATHAN HARKER’S JOURNAL

recaps.text: Jonathan Harker escaped Count Dracula's castle and fell ill, while the Count shipped fifty boxes of earth to London. In London Lucy Westenra sleepwalked, weakened and died after transfusions, and her mother had died earlier. Children on Hampstead Heath were found with throat wounds, which Van Helsing blamed on Lucy, Un-Dead; the men staked her body and resolved to destroy the Count. They searched the Carfax house and traced removed boxes to a house in Piccadilly, bought by a Count de Ville. That night Renfield was found gravely injured after a struggle, and he told how the Count came to his window and how he tried to save Mrs. Harker. The men burst into the Harkers' room and found the Count feeding on Mina while Jonathan lay in a stupor; the Count fled. Mina has now told of the attack and of being bound to the Count's call. The men are gathering to plan their next move as dawn comes, with Mina and Jonathan in their care and the Count still at large.

Seward finds Renfield gravely injured on the floor, and Van Helsing decides to trephine him to relieve the pressure from his brain. Renfield wakes briefly and tells how the Count came to his window and how he tried to stop him from drawing life from Mrs. Harker. Hearing the commotion, Van Helsing, Seward, Godalming and Morris arm themselves and burst into the Harkers' room. They find the Count feeding on Mina while Jonathan lies in a stupor, and the Count flees as the men raise their sacred objects. Jonathan is woken and Mina, horrified by her wound and her own uncleanness, pulls away from him before he insists on staying close. Godalming reports that the Count burned the manuscript and phonograph cylinders and that Renfield is dead. Morris reports that the Count likely went to another hiding place, and dawn approaches with the men resolving to act the next day. Mina recounts the Count's attack, how he drank her blood and forced her to drink from his breast, binding her to his call.
recaps.title: CHAPTER XXI DR. SEWARD’S DIARY

recaps.text: Jonathan Harker escaped Count Dracula's castle and fell ill, while the Count shipped fifty boxes of earth to London. Lucy Westenra sleepwalked, weakened and died after transfusions, and her mother had died earlier. Children on Hampstead Heath were found with throat wounds, which Van Helsing blamed on Lucy, Un-Dead; the men staked her body and resolved to destroy the Count. They searched Carfax and traced boxes to a Piccadilly house. That night Renfield was found dead, and the men burst in on the Count feeding on Mina; the Count fled. Mina has told of the attack and of being bound to the Count's call. This morning Seward certifies Renfield's death as an accident, and Van Helsing marks Mina's forehead with the Sacred Wafer, which burns and leaves a scar she believes makes her unclean. The men swear to protect her, then sterilise Carfax's earth-boxes and enter the Piccadilly house, finding eight of nine boxes. Godalming and Morris take the keys to destroy the remaining lairs, while the rest wait in the house for the Count or their return. The ninth box and the Count remain unfound, and Mina's safety and fate are unresolved.

Renfield is found dead, and Seward plans to certify the death as an accident. Van Helsing and the group agree Mina must know everything, and she vows to live rather than die by her own hand. The group decides to sterilise the Count's lairs and search the Piccadilly house, which they believe holds the key to the Count's houses and belongings. Van Helsing burns the Sacred Wafer onto Mina's forehead, and she collapses in despair believing she is unclean. The men kneel with Mina and Jonathan and swear to protect her, then set out for Carfax. At Carfax the group sterilises the earth-boxes with pieces of the Host. Godalming and Morris hire a locksmith to open the Piccadilly house while the others wait nearby. Inside the Piccadilly house they find eight of the nine earth-boxes, plus deeds, keys and writing materials. Godalming and Morris take the keys to destroy the remaining lairs, while the others wait for them or for the Count.
recaps.title: CHAPTER XXII JONATHAN HARKER’S JOURNAL

recaps.text: Jonathan Harker escaped Count Dracula's castle and fell ill, while the Count shipped fifty boxes of earth to London. Lucy Westenra died after transfusions and was staked as Un-Dead, and the men resolved to destroy the Count. They found and sterilised most of his earth-boxes, Renfield died, and the Count fled from the Piccadilly house. Mina was bitten and now bears a burning mark on her forehead, and the men have sworn to protect her. Godalming and Morris destroyed the remaining lairs at Bermondsey and Mile End. The Count burst into Seward's house, was struck by Harker, and escaped through the window. Under hypnosis Mina revealed the Count is on a ship at anchor, fleeing London by sea. The men now plan to follow him, though Mina fears she is marked and her husband is grief-stricken. Unresolved: the ninth earth-box, the ship's destination, and Mina's fate.

Godalming and Morris return reporting the earth-boxes at two places have been destroyed. Mina's telegram warns that the Count has left Carfax and is heading south. The Count bursts into the room and Harker strikes at him with his knife, but he escapes through the window and vanishes into the stable. Van Helsing reads the Count's flight as fear, concluding he means to escape London by sea. Mina asks to be hypnotised before dawn, and under it she reports being on a ship at anchor. The men realise the Count has taken his last earth-box aboard a vessel and is leaving the land. Van Helsing warns Mina that the mark on her throat means she must be pursued, since the Count can live for centuries. Mina faints as the danger to her is made clear, and the search for the Count goes on.
recaps.title: CHAPTER XXIII DR. SEWARD’S DIARY

recaps.text: Jonathan Harker escaped Count Dracula's castle and fell ill, while the Count shipped boxes of earth to London. Lucy Westenra died after transfusions and was staked as Un-Dead, and the men resolved to destroy the Count. They found and destroyed his earth-boxes, Renfield died, and the Count fled from the Piccadilly house. Mina was bitten and bears a burning mark on her forehead; the men swore to protect her. The Count burst into Seward's house, was struck by Harker, and escaped. Under hypnosis Mina revealed the Count is aboard a ship at anchor. The men have now traced him to the Czarina Catherine, bound for Varna with a box of earth, and plan to reach Varna overland first. Mina insists on joining them, and Harker, bound by a promise not to be told the plans, is preparing to travel. Unresolved: the ninth earth-box, the ship's arrival, and Mina's fate.

Van Helsing reports that the Count is returning to Transylvania and that his escape can be traced to a ship. The party learns the Czarina Catherine left the Thames for Varna carrying a box of earth and a tall, pale stranger. They plan to reach Varna overland before the ship, arming themselves with Winchesters and wild rose. Mina insists on joining the pursuit, fearing the Count may command her and that she could betray their plans. Harker is told he must stay behind to guard his wife, but he agrees to consider it with her. Mina secures a promise from Harker not to tell her anything of the plans, and he gives it. Van Helsing decides Mina will travel with them, and the men resolve to destroy the Count at Varna. Harker sets his affairs in order and makes his will, leaving Mina his heir.
recaps.title: CHAPTER XXIV DR. SEWARD’S PHONOGRAPH DIARY, SPOKEN BY VAN HELSING

recaps.text: Jonathan Harker escaped Count Dracula's castle and fell ill while the Count shipped earth-boxes to London. Lucy Westenra died and was staked as Un-Dead, and the men destroyed the Count's earth-boxes and drove him from the Piccadilly house. Mina was bitten and bears a mark on her forehead. Under hypnosis, Mina revealed the Count's ship, and the party traced him to the Czarina Catherine. The party waited at Varna for the ship, then learned it had reached Galatz. The party plans to leave for Galatz on the 6:30 train, and Van Helsing believes Mina's connection to the Count may aid them. Unresolved: the ninth earth-box, the Count's whereabouts, and Mina's fate.

The party learns the Czarina Catherine has reached Galatz, meaning the Count has escaped them on the ship. Mina's trance reports and telegrams keep the party waiting at Varna until the ship's arrival is announced. Van Helsing and Seward worry over Mina's lethargy and the possibility of her changing, though they say nothing to the others. Mina reveals she knows the train schedule to Galatz, and the party resolves to leave at dawn. Van Helsing assigns each man a task to prepare for the journey and the boarding of the ship. Van Helsing reasons that the Count's selfish criminal nature has led him to flee, and that Mina's link to him may help the group.
recaps.title: CHAPTER XXV DR. SEWARD’S DIARY

recaps.text: Jonathan Harker escaped Count Dracula's castle and fell ill while the Count shipped earth-boxes to London. Lucy Westenra died and was staked as Un-Dead, and the men destroyed the Count's earth-boxes and drove him from the Piccadilly house. Mina was bitten and bears a mark on her forehead. Under hypnosis, Mina revealed the Count's ship, and the party traced him to the Czarina Catherine, which reached Galatz. At Galatz the box was handed to Skinsky, who was then found murdered. Mina deduced that the box was carried up a river toward the Count's castle. Lord Godalming and Jonathan follow by launch, Dr. Seward and Quincey Morris ride the banks, and Van Helsing takes Mina overland toward the Borgo Pass. The box, the Count's whereabouts and Mina's fate remain unresolved.

Mina reports under hypnosis that the box is near land, but her readings grow uncertain and her power may be failing. At Galatz the party learns from Captain Donelson and Hildesheim that the box passed to Skinsky before sunrise. Skinsky is later found murdered in a churchyard, leaving the party without a trail for the box. Mina deduces from her trance and the maps that the box travelled up the Sereth or Pruth toward the Count's castle. Lord Godalming and Jonathan take a steam launch up the river, while Dr. Seward and Quincey Morris ride the banks. Van Helsing decides to take Mina overland through the Borgo Pass, despite Jonathan's fierce objections. Jonathan agrees, and Mina and Van Helsing set off for Veresti to buy a carriage and horses. The river pursuit reaches the Bistritza, where the party searches boats but has not yet found the box.
recaps.title: CHAPTER XXVI DR. SEWARD’S DIARY

recaps.text: Van Helsing and Mina travel through the Borgo Pass toward the Count's castle, guided by Mina's knowledge from Jonathan's journal. At night three female figures materialise and call Mina to join them, but she stays within the holy circle. Van Helsing goes alone to the castle and destroys the three Un-Dead women and the Count's tomb, then he and Mina head east. Mina and Van Helsing shelter in rock and see the gypsy cart racing toward sunset with the men in pursuit. Jonathan, Godalming, Seward and Morris halt the gypsies and break open the Count's box. Jonathan and Morris strike the Count, who crumbles to dust as the sun sets.

This closing note, written years after the events, reflects on the survivors' lives and their pride in the son named after Quincey Morris. The companions revisit Transylvania and find the castle unchanged in its desolation, confirming their memories as real. Back home they admit their written record would not convince an outsider, and Van Helsing says that proof is unnecessary.
